Though the medical specialty of psychiatry uses research in the field of [[neuroscience]], [[psychology]], [[medicine]], [[biology]], [[biochemistry]], and [[pharmacology]],<ref name=Pietrini>{{cite journal|vauthors=Pietrini P|title=Toward a biochemistry of mind?|journal=The American Journal of Psychiatry|volume=160|issue=11|pages=1907–8|date=November 2003|pmid=14594732|doi=10.1176/appi.ajp.160.11.1907|doi-access=free|department=Editorial}}</ref> it has generally been considered a middle ground between [[neurology]] and psychology.{{sfn|Shorter|1997|p=326}} Because psychiatry and neurology are deeply intertwined medical specialties, all certification in the United States for both specialties and for their subspecialties is offered by a single board, the American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology, one of the member boards of the American Board of Medical Specialties.<ref>{{citation|title=Specialty and Subspecialty Certificates|date=n.d.|website=American Board of Medical Specialties|url=http://www.abms.org/member-boards/specialty-subspecialty-certificates/|access-date=27 July 2016|archive-date=23 January 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200123231140/https://www.abms.org/member-boards/specialty-subspecialty-certificates/|url-status=live}}</ref> Unlike other physicians and neurologists, psychiatrists specialize in the [[doctor–patient relationship]] and are trained to varying extents in the use of psychotherapy and other therapeutic communication techniques.{{sfn|Shorter|1997|p=326}} Psychiatrists also differ from psychologists in that they are physicians and have postgraduate training called residency (usually four to five years) in psychiatry; the quality and thoroughness of their graduate medical training is identical to that of all other physicians.<ref name=Hauser>{{cite web| vauthors = Hauser MJ |title=Student Information |url= http://www.psychiatry.com/student.php |website=Psychiatry.com|access-date=21 September 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101023095258/http://www.psychiatry.com/student.php|archive-date=23 October 2010}}</ref> Psychiatrists can therefore counsel patients, prescribe medication, order [[medical laboratory|laboratory test]]s, order [[neuroimaging]], and conduct [[physical examination]]s.<ref name=NIMHSite>{{cite web|publisher=National Institute of Mental Health|date=January 31, 2006|title=Information about Mental Illness and the Brain (Page 3 of 3)|website=The Science of Mental Illness|access-date=April 19, 2007|url=http://science-education.nih.gov/supplements/nih5/Mental/guide/info-mental-c.htm|archive-date=12 October 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071012140052/http://science-education.nih.gov/supplements/nih5/Mental/guide/info-mental-c.htm}}</ref> As well, some psychiatrists are trained in [[interventional psychiatry]] and can deliver interventional treatments such as [[electroconvulsive therapy]], [[transcranial magnetic stimulation]], [[vagus nerve stimulation]] and [[ketamine]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-07-27 |title=Handbook of Interventional Psychiatry - Handbook of Interventional Psychiatry |url=https://interventionalpsych.org/ |access-date=2024-08-28 |website=interventionalpsych.org |language=en-US}}</ref>

===Ethics===
{{See also|Ethical issues in psychiatry (disambiguation)}}
The [[World Psychiatric Association]] issues an [[ethical code]] to govern the conduct of psychiatrists (like other purveyors of [[professional ethics]]). The psychiatric code of ethics, first set forth through the Declaration of Hawaii in 1977 has been expanded through a 1983 Vienna update and in the broader Madrid Declaration in 1996. The code was further revised during the organization's general assemblies in 1999, 2002, 2005, and 2011.<ref name=WPAethics>{{cite web|date=21 September 2011|title=Madrid Declaration on Ethical Standards for Psychiatric Practice|url=http://wpanet.org/detail.php?section_id=5&content_id=48|website=World Psychiatric Association|access-date=3 November 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304140238/http://wpanet.org/detail.php?section_id=5&content_id=48|archive-date=4 March 2016}}</ref>

The World Psychiatric Association code covers such matters as [[confidentiality]], the [[Capital punishment|death penalty]], ethnic or cultural discrimination,<ref name="WPAethics" /> [[euthanasia]], genetics, the [[dignity|human dignity]] of incapacitated patients, media relations, organ transplantation, patient assessment, research ethics, sex selection,<ref name="Lopez">{{cite journal|vauthors=López-Muñoz F, Alamo C, Dudley M, Rubio G, García-García P, Molina JD, Okasha A|title=Psychiatry and political-institutional abuse from the historical perspective: the ethical lessons of the Nuremberg Trial on their 60th anniversary|journal=Progress in Neuro-Psychopharmacology & Biological Psychiatry|volume=31|issue=4|pages=791–806|date=May 2007|pmid=17223241|doi=10.1016/j.pnpbp.2006.12.007|quote=These practices, in which racial hygiene constituted one of the fundamental principles and euthanasia programmes were the most obvious consequence, violated the majority of known bioethical principles. Psychiatry played a central role in these programmes, and the mentally ill were the principal victims.|others=Cecilio Alamoa, Michael Dudleyb, Gabriel Rubioc, Pilar García-Garcíaa, Juan D. Molinad and Ahmed Okasha|s2cid=39675837}}</ref> [[coercion]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Herrman |first1=Helen |last2=Allan |first2=John |last3=Galderisi |first3=Silvana |last4=Javed |first4=Afzal |last5=Rodrigues |first5=Maria |last6=the WPA Task Force on Implementing Alternatives to Coercion in Mental Health Care |date=2022-01-11 |title=Alternatives to coercion in mental health care: WPA Position Statement and Call to Action |journal=World Psychiatry |language=en |volume=21 |issue=1 |pages=159–160 |doi=10.1002/wps.20950 |pmid=35015368 |pmc=8751569 }}</ref> [[torture]],<ref name="Gluzman">{{cite journal|vauthors=Gluzman SF|title=Abuse of psychiatry: analysis of the guilt of medical personnel|journal=Journal of Medical Ethics|volume=17 Suppl|issue=Suppl|pages=19–20|date=December 1991|pmid=1795363|pmc=1378165|doi=10.1136/jme.17.Suppl.19|quote=Based on the generally accepted definition, we correctly term the utilisation of psychiatry for the punishment of political dissidents as torture.|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Debreu">{{cite book|chapter-url=http://books.nap.edu/openbook.php?record_id=9733&page=21|vauthors=Debreu G|veditors=Corillon C|title=Science and Human Rights|chapter=Introduction|page=21|access-date=2007-10-04|year=1988|publisher=The National Academies Press|url=https://www.nap.edu/catalog/9733/science-and-human-rights|doi=10.17226/9733|pmid=25077249|bibcode=1988nap..book.9733N |doi-access=free|quote=Over the past two decades the systematic use of torture and psychiatric abuse have been sanctioned or condoned by more than one-third of the nations in the United Nations, about half of mankind.|isbn=978-0-309-57510-2|archive-date=2015-09-10|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150910065933/http://www.nap.edu/catalog/9733/science-and-human-rights|url-status=live}}</ref> and up-to-date knowledge.

In establishing such ethical codes, the profession has responded to a number of controversies about the practice of psychiatry, for example, surrounding the use of [[lobotomy]] and [[electroconvulsive therapy]].

Discredited psychiatrists who operated outside the norms of [[medical ethics]] include [[Harry Bailey]], [[Donald Ewen Cameron]], [[Samuel A. Cartwright]], [[Henry Cotton (doctor)|Henry Cotton]], and [[Andrei Snezhnevsky]].<ref name="Kirk2013">{{cite book| vauthors = Kirk S, Gomory T, Cohen D |title=Mad Science: Psychiatric Coercion, Diagnosis, and Drugs|year=2013|publisher=Transaction Publishers|location=New Brunswick, NJ|oclc=935892629|isbn=978-1-4128-4976-0}}</ref>{{Page needed|date=March 2015}}

===Approaches===
Psychiatric illnesses can be conceptualised in several different ways. The [[biomedical model|biomedical]] approach examines signs and symptoms and compares them with diagnostic criteria. Mental illness can be assessed, conversely, through a narrative which tries to incorporate symptoms into a meaningful life history and to frame them as responses to external conditions.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Atkinson |first1=Tess M. |last2=Nathan |first2=Leigh |last3=Sukhera |first3=Javeed I. |title=The Power Threat Meaning Framework: A Socially Conscious Shift in the Conceptualization of Mental and Physical Health |journal=Journal of Prevention and Health Promotion |date=November 2025 |volume=6 |issue=4 |pages=591–615 |doi=10.1177/26320770251351955}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Melani |first1=Marina S. |last2=Paiva |first2=Jéssica M. |last3=da Silva |first3=Herika C. |last4=Mendes |first4=Thais P. |last5=Pereira |first5=Brunno G. |last6=Lobo |first6=Isabela |last7=Berger |first7=William |title=From turmoil to transformation: A systematic review of peritraumatic reactions and posttraumatic growth |journal=European Journal of Trauma & Dissociation |date=June 2026 |volume=10 |issue=2 |article-number=100673 |doi=10.1016/j.ejtd.2026.100673}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Frøkedal |first1=Hilde |last2=Lloyd |first2=Christina |last3=Halstensen |first3=Kari |last4=Hammersbøen |first4=Åse Marit |last5=Austad |first5=Anne |title=The Use of Existential Groups in Mental Health Care: A Scoping Review |journal=International Journal of Group Psychotherapy |date=2 January 2026 |volume=76 |issue=1 |pages=33–100 |doi=10.1080/00207284.2025.2551501 |pmid=41026634 }}</ref> 
For example, the Power Threat Meaning Framework (PTMF) is a conceptual approach to understanding mental distress that serves as an alternative to traditional psychiatric diagnostic systems.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Harper |first1=D J |title=De-medicalising public mental health with the Power Threat Meaning Framework |journal=Perspectives in Public Health |date=May 2023 |volume=143 |issue=3 |pages=151–155 |doi=10.1177/17579139231157531 |pmid=37132024 |url=https://repository.uel.ac.uk/download/bbc36c9e284f9809436752c18b43d24f1570168f516c1f8ea72be26417917769/449466/PTMF%20Demedicalising%20PMH%20ACCEPTED.pdf }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Johnstone |first1=Lucy |last2=Boyle |first2=Mary |title=The Power Threat Meaning Framework: An Alternative Nondiagnostic Conceptual System |journal=Journal of Humanistic Psychology |date=July 2025 |volume=65 |issue=4 |pages=800–817 |doi=10.1177/0022167818793289}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Atkinson |first1=Tess M. |last2=Nathan |first2=Leigh |last3=Sukhera |first3=Javeed I. |title=The Power Threat Meaning Framework: A Socially Conscious Shift in the Conceptualization of Mental and Physical Health |journal=Journal of Prevention and Health Promotion |date=November 2025 |volume=6 |issue=4 |pages=591–615 |doi=10.1177/26320770251351955}}</ref>  Rather than viewing distress primarily as a symptom of an underlying mental disorder, the framework emphasizes the role of adversity, trauma, social inequalities, relationships, and cultural contexts in shaping people's experiences, and proposes that many forms of distress can be understood as meaningful responses to difficult circumstances.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Harper |first1=D J |title=De-medicalising public mental health with the Power Threat Meaning Framework |journal=Perspectives in Public Health |date=May 2023 |volume=143 |issue=3 |pages=151–155 |doi=10.1177/17579139231157531 |pmid=37132024 |url=https://repository.uel.ac.uk/download/bbc36c9e284f9809436752c18b43d24f1570168f516c1f8ea72be26417917769/449466/PTMF%20Demedicalising%20PMH%20ACCEPTED.pdf }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Johnstone |first1=Lucy |last2=Boyle |first2=Mary |title=The Power Threat Meaning Framework: An Alternative Nondiagnostic Conceptual System |journal=Journal of Humanistic Psychology |date=July 2025 |volume=65 |issue=4 |pages=800–817 |doi=10.1177/0022167818793289}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Atkinson |first1=Tess M. |last2=Nathan |first2=Leigh |last3=Sukhera |first3=Javeed I. |title=The Power Threat Meaning Framework: A Socially Conscious Shift in the Conceptualization of Mental and Physical Health |journal=Journal of Prevention and Health Promotion |date=November 2025 |volume=6 |issue=4 |pages=591–615 |doi=10.1177/26320770251351955}}</ref>

Both approaches are considered important in the field of psychiatry, but have not sufficiently reconciled to settle [[biopsychiatry controversy|controversy]] over either the selection of a psychiatric [[paradigm]] or the specification of [[psychopathology]]. The [[biopsychosocial model]] is used to explain the multifactorial origins of clinical impairment, recognizing that biological, psychological, and social factors all play a role in health and disease.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wolfe |first1=Rebecca |last2=Speakar |first2=Brianna |last3=Pham |first3=Mai |last4=Lorenz |first4=Tierney |last5=Spaulding |first5=William |title=The past and future of integrated biopsychosocial whole-health perspectives in psychiatric rehabilitation. |journal=Psychiatric Rehabilitation Journal |date=March 2026 |volume=49 |issue=1 |pages=66–78 |doi=10.1037/prj0000682 |pmid=41569515 |pmc=12829903 }}</ref><ref name= Karunamuni2020 >{{cite journal |author= Karunamuni N, Imayama I, Goonetilleke D. |title= Pathways to well-being: Untangling the causal relationships among biopsychosocial variables |journal= Social Science & Medicine |date= 2021 |volume= 272 |article-number= 112846 | doi= 10.1016/j.socscimed.2020.112846 |pmid= 32089388 }}</ref><ref name="Nakao2020">{{Cite journal |last1=Nakao |first1=Mutsuhiro |last2=Komaki |first2=Gen |last3=Yoshiuchi |first3=Kazuhiro |last4=Deter |first4=Hans-Christian |last5=Fukudo |first5=Shin |date=2020-12-08 |title=Biopsychosocial medicine research trends: connecting clinical medicine, psychology, and public health |journal=BioPsychoSocial Medicine |volume=14 |issue=1 |page=30 |doi=10.1186/s13030-020-00204-9 |issn=1751-0759 |pmc=7722433 |pmid=33292438 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

Once a medical professional diagnoses a patient there are numerous ways that they could choose to treat the patient. Often psychiatrists will develop a treatment strategy that incorporates different facets of different approaches into one. Drug prescriptions are very commonly written to be regimented to patients along with any therapy they receive. There are three major pillars of psychotherapy that treatment strategies are most regularly drawn from. [[Humanistic psychology]] attempts to put the "whole" of the patient in perspective; it also focuses on self exploration.<ref name="humanistic">{{cite web| vauthors = Michael H |title=Humanistic Therapy|website=CRC Health Group.|access-date=29 March 2015|url=http://www.crchealth.com/types-of-therapy/what-is-humanistic-therapy|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190602153855/https://www.crchealth.com/types-of-therapy/what-is-humanistic-therapy|archive-date=2 June 2019}}</ref> [[Behaviorism]] is a therapeutic school of thought that elects to focus solely on real and observable events, rather than mining the unconscious or ''subconscious''. [[Psychoanalysis]], on the other hand, concentrates its dealings on early childhood, irrational drives, the unconscious, and conflict between conscious and unconscious streams.<ref name="psychoanalysis">{{cite web|vauthors=McLeod S|date=2014|title=Psychoanalysis|website=Simply Psychology|access-date=29 March 2015|url=http://www.simplypsychology.org/psychoanalysis.html|archive-date=19 April 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150419052206/http://www.simplypsychology.org/psychoanalysis.html|url-status=live}}</ref> In recent years, [[mindfulness]] practices involving present-moment awareness have gained popularity and have been shown to be effective in psychiatric treatment.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Alkan |first1=Ekin |last2=Kumar |first2=Geetanjali ===Practitioners===
{{Main|Psychiatrist}}
{{One source section|date=August 2017}}
All [[physician]]s can diagnose mental disorders and prescribe treatments utilizing principles of psychiatry. [[Psychiatrist]]s are trained physicians who specialize in psychiatry and are certified to treat [[mental illness]]. They may treat outpatients, inpatients, or both; they may practice as solo practitioners or as members of groups; they may be self-employed, be members of partnerships, or be employees of governmental, academic, nonprofit, or for-profit entities; employees of hospitals; they may treat military personnel as civilians or as members of the military; and in any of these settings they may function as clinicians, researchers, teachers, or some combination of these. Although psychiatrists may also go through significant training to conduct [[psychotherapy]], [[psychoanalysis]] or [[cognitive behavioral therapy]], it is their training as physicians that differentiates them from other [[mental health professional]]s.

====As a career choice in the US====
Psychiatry was not a popular career choice among medical students, even though medical school placements are rated favorably.<ref name="link.springer.com">{{cite journal|vauthors=Brown M, Barnes J, Silver K, Williams N, Newton PM|title=The Educational Impact of Exposure to Clinical Psychiatry Early in an Undergraduate Medical Curriculum|journal=Academic Psychiatry|volume=40|issue=2|pages=274–81|date=April 2016|pmid=26077010|doi=10.1007/s40596-015-0358-1|s2cid=13274934}}</ref> This has resulted in a significant shortage of psychiatrists in the United States and elsewhere.<ref>{{cite web|vauthors=Japsen B|date=15 September 2015|title=Psychiatrist Shortage Worsens Amid 'Mental Health Crisis'|website=Forbes|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/brucejapsen/2015/09/15/psychiatrist-shortage-worsens-amid-mental-health-crisis/|access-date=8 September 2017|archive-date=9 September 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170909004934/https://www.forbes.com/sites/brucejapsen/2015/09/15/psychiatrist-shortage-worsens-amid-mental-health-crisis/|url-status=live}}</ref> Strategies to address this shortfall have included the use of short 'taster' placements early in the medical school curriculum<ref name="link.springer.com"/> and attempts to extend psychiatry services further using [[telemedicine]] technologies and other methods.<ref name=THIELE>{{cite journal|vauthors=Thiele JS, Doarn CR, Shore JH|title=Locum tenens and telepsychiatry: trends in psychiatric care|journal=Telemedicine Journal and e-Health|volume=21|issue=6|pages=510–3|date=June 2015|pmid=25764147|doi=10.1089/tmj.2014.0159|doi-access=free}}</ref> Recently, however, there has been an increase in the number of medical students entering into a psychiatry residency. There are several reasons for this surge, including the intriguing nature of the field, growing interest in [[psychiatric genetics|genetic biomarkers involved]] in psychiatric diagnoses, and newer pharmaceuticals on the drug market to treat psychiatric illnesses.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1176/appi.pn.2015.4b15|title=2015 Match Finds Big Jump in Students Choosing Psychiatry |journal=Psychiatric News |volume=50|issue=8|page=1|year=2015| vauthors = Moran M }}</ref>

[[Addiction psychiatry]] focuses on evaluation and treatment of individuals with alcohol, drug, or other substance-related disorders, and of individuals with dual diagnosis of substance-related and other psychiatric disorders. [[Biological psychiatry]] is an approach to psychiatry that aims to understand mental disorders in terms of the biological function of the nervous system. [[Child and adolescent psychiatry]] is the branch of psychiatry that specializes in work with children, teenagers, and their families. [[Community psychiatry]] is an approach that reflects an inclusive [[public health]] perspective and is practiced in [[community mental health services]].<ref>{{cite web|website=American Association of Community Psychiatrists|url=http://www.comm.psych.pitt.edu/mission.html|publisher=University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine, Department of Psychiatry|title=About AACP|access-date=August 5, 2008|archive-date=6 September 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090906041751/http://www.comm.psych.pitt.edu/mission.html}}</ref> [[Cross-cultural psychiatry]] is a branch of psychiatry concerned with the cultural and ethnic context of mental disorder and psychiatric services. [[Emergency psychiatry]] is the clinical application of psychiatry in emergency settings. [[Forensic psychiatry]] utilizes medical science generally, and psychiatric knowledge and assessment methods in particular, to help answer legal questions. [[Geriatric psychiatry]] is a branch of psychiatry dealing with the study, prevention, and treatment of mental disorders in the [[Old age|elderly]]. [[Global mental health]] is an area of study, research and practice that places a priority on improving mental health and achieving equity in mental health for all people worldwide,<ref name="Patel">{{cite journal|vauthors=Patel V, Prince M|title=Global mental health: a new global health field comes of age|journal=JAMA|volume=303|issue=19|pages=1976–7|date=May 2010|pmid=20483977|pmc=3432444|doi=10.1001/jama.2010.616|department=Commentary}}</ref> although some scholars consider it to be a neo-colonial, culturally insensitive project.<ref>{{cite book|title=Decolonizing Global Mental Health: The Psychiatrization of the Majority World | last1= Mills |first1=C |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-84872-160-9|location=London|oclc=837146781|date=2013-11-11}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=Crazy like us| vauthors = Watters E |isbn=978-1-84901-577-6|location=London|oclc=751584971|year=2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=Mental health, race and culture| vauthors = Suman F |date=2010|publisher=Palgrave Macmillan|isbn=978-0-230-21271-8|edition=3rd|location=Basingstoke, Hampshire|oclc=455800587}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=Mental health worldwide: culture, globalization and development| vauthors = Suman F |isbn=978-1-137-32958-5|location=Houndmills, Basingstoke, Hampshire|oclc=869802072|date=2014-04-11}}</ref> [[Liaison psychiatry]] is the branch of psychiatry that specializes in the interface between other medical specialties and psychiatry. [[Military psychiatry]] covers special aspects of psychiatry and mental disorders within the military context. [[Neuropsychiatry]] is a branch of medicine dealing with mental disorders attributable to diseases of the nervous system. [[Social psychiatry]] is a branch of psychiatry that focuses on the interpersonal and cultural context of mental disorder and mental well-being. [[Evolutionary psychiatry]] (or Darwinian psychiatry) is a theoretical orientation within psychiatry that applies principles from evolutionary biology—such as natural selection, adaptation, mismatch, and trade‑offs—to frame hypotheses about the origins, persistence, and variation of mental disorders.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Abed |first1=Riadh |last2=Brüne |first2=Martin |last3=Wilson |first3=Daniel R. |date=October 2019 |title=The role of the evolutionary approach in psychiatry |journal=World Psychiatry |language=en |volume=18 |issue=3 |pages=370–371 |doi=10.1002/wps.20688 |issn=1723-8617 |pmc=6732701 |pmid=31496100}}</ref>

In larger healthcare organizations, psychiatrists often serve in senior management roles, where they are responsible for the efficient and effective delivery of mental health services for the organization's constituents. For example, the chief of mental health services at most VA medical centers is usually a psychiatrist, although psychologists occasionally are selected for the position as well.{{citation needed|date=May 2013}}

In the United States, psychiatry is one of the few specialties which qualify for further education and board-certification in [[pain management|pain medicine]], [[palliative care|palliative medicine]], and [[sleep medicine]].

===Research===
Psychiatric research is, by its very nature, interdisciplinary; combining social, biological and psychological perspectives in attempt to understand the nature and treatment of mental disorders.<ref name=UManchester>{{cite web|website=University of Manchester|title=Research in Psychiatry|access-date=13 October 2007|url=http://www.manchester.ac.uk/research/areas/subareas/?a=s&id=44694|archive-date=23 December 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071223064538/http://www.manchester.ac.uk/research/areas/subareas/?a=s&id=44694}}</ref> Clinical and research psychiatrists study basic and clinical psychiatric topics at research institutions and publish articles in journals.<ref name=Pietrini/><ref name=NYSPI>{{cite web|title=New York State Psychiatric Institute|date=15 March 2007|access-date=13 October 2007|url=http://nyspi.org/|archive-date=5 November 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201105232057/https://nyspi.org/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=CPRF>{{cite web|title=Canadian Psychiatric Research Foundation|date=27 July 2007|access-date=13 October 2007|url=http://www.cprf.ca/|archive-date=10 October 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071010110827/http://www.cprf.ca/}}</ref><ref name=Elsevier>{{cite web|website=Elsevier|date=8 October 2007|title=Journal of Psychiatric Research|access-date=13 October 2007|url=http://www.elsevier.com/wps/find/journaldescription.cws_home/241/description|archive-date=30 September 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200930221852/https://www.elsevier.com/journals/journal-of-psychiatric-research/0022-3956|url-status=live}}</ref> Under the supervision of [[institutional review board]]s, psychiatric clinical researchers look at topics such as neuroimaging, genetics, and psychopharmacology in order to enhance diagnostic validity and reliability, to discover new treatment methods, and to classify new mental disorders.<ref name=Mitchell>{{cite book|vauthors=Mitchell JE, Crosby RD, Wonderlich SA, Adson DE|date=2000|title=Elements of Clinical Research in Psychiatry|url=https://archive.org/details/elementsofclinic0000unse|url-access=registration|location=Washington, DC|publisher=American Psychiatric Press|isbn=978-0-88048-802-0|oclc=632834662}}</ref>{{Page needed|date=August 2017}}

Another thing to consider in research and conducting research in the field of psychiatry is the patients needs and values as Brock<ref>Brock, D. W. (1993). Informed consent. In ''Life and Death: Philosophical Essays in Biomedical Ethics'' (pp. 21-54). Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511625350</ref> mentions their chapter on ''Informed Consent'' regarding the need to explain and inform participants about a research study and also act in their best interests, as Hellman and Hellman discuss.<ref>Hellman, S., & Hellman, D. S. (1991). Of Mice but Not Men: Problems of the Randomized Clinical Trial. ''The New England Journal of Medicine, 324''(22), 1585–1589. https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM199105303242208</ref> This can face challenges, such as dual-conflict roles in which their conflict roles between being a doctor and a researcher, especially in research involving control groups where some participants are not getting a treatment, where treating people as a merely just a means to an end, as discussed in Kantian morals, and not prioritizing their well-being and ensuring they are informed and given the option of treatments available, even those in research with positive predicted outcomes.<ref>Hellman, S., & Hellman, D. S. (1991). Of Mice but Not Men: Problems of the Randomized Clinical Trial. ''The New England Journal of Medicine, 324''(22), 1585–1589. https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM199105303242208</ref> Moreover, when considering participants in research, it is also important to look at labelling and stigma attached as published research can be read and used by the public and cause bias, despite research limitations if they are not addressed and thought-out thoroughly by a reader, and cause people to push labels on people, as Voronka discusses how research can be used and influenced to make homelessness mental health condition instead of a result of structural and capitalist policies,<ref>
  Voronka, J. (2019). Slow Death through Evidence-Based Research. In L. Costa, A. Daley, & P. Beresford (Eds.), ''Madness, Violence, and Power'' (pp. 80–96). University of Toronto Press. https://doi.org/10.3138/9781442629981-011
</ref> as well as can create a stigma around people deemed so-called at-risk, as Corcoran, Malaspina, and Hercher discuss,<ref>
  Corcoran, C., Malaspina, D., & Hercher, L. (2005). Prodromal interventions for schizophrenia vulnerability: the risks of being "at risk." ''Schizophrenia Research'', 73(2), 173–184. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.schres.2004.05.021
</ref> raising questions around when to intervene and how research can be harmful.

==Diagnostics and evaluation==

=== Present ===

==== Diagnostic systems ====
{{see also|Diagnostic classification and rating scales used in psychiatry}}
[[Psychiatric assessment|Psychiatric diagnoses]] take place in a wide variety of settings and are performed by many different [[health care provider|health professionals]]. Therefore, the diagnostic procedure may vary greatly based upon these factors. Typically, though, a psychiatric diagnosis utilizes a [[differential diagnosis]] procedure where a [[mental status examination]] and physical examination is conducted, with [[pathological]], [[psychopathological]] or [[psychosocial]] histories obtained, and sometimes [[neuroimaging|neuroimages]] or other [[neurophysiological]] measurements are taken, or [[personality test]]s or [[cognitive test]]s administered.<ref name=Meyendorf>{{cite journal|vauthors=Meyendorf R|title=[Diagnosis and differential diagnosis in psychiatry and the question of situation referred prognostic diagnosis]|language=de|journal=Schweizer Archiv für Neurologie, Neurochirurgie und Psychiatrie = Archives Suisses de Neurologie, Neurochirurgie et de Psychiatrie|volume=126|issue=1|pages=121–34|year=1980|pmid=7414302|trans-title=Diagnosis and differential diagnosis in psychiatry and the question of situation referred prognostic diagnosis}}</ref><ref>{{cite book| vauthors = Leigh H |date=1983|title=Psychiatry in the practice of medicine|location=Menlo Park, CA|publisher=Addison-Wesley|isbn=978-0-201-05456-9|pages=[https://archive.org/details/psychiatryinprac0000unse/page/15 15, 17, 67]|oclc=869194520|url=https://archive.org/details/psychiatryinprac0000unse/page/15}}</ref>{{sfn|Lyness|1997|p=10}}<ref name=Hampel>{{cite journal|vauthors=Hampel H, Teipel SJ, Kötter HU, Horwitz B, Pfluger T, Mager T, Möller HJ, Müller-Spahn F|title=[Structural magnetic resonance tomography in diagnosis and research of Alzheimer type dementia]|language=de|journal=Der Nervenarzt|volume=68|issue=5|pages=365–78|date=May 1997|pmid=9280846|doi=10.1007/s001150050138|s2cid=35203096|trans-title=Structural magnetic resonance imaging in diagnosis and research of Alzheimer's disease}}</ref><ref name=Townsend>{{cite journal| vauthors = Townsend BA, Petrella JR, Doraiswamy PM |date=July 2002|title=The role of neuroimaging in geriatric psychiatry|journal=Current Opinion in Psychiatry|volume=15|issue=4|pages=427–32|doi=10.1097/00001504-200207000-00014|s2cid=147489857}}</ref> In some cases, a brain scan might be used to rule out other medical illnesses, but at this time relying on brain scans alone cannot accurately diagnose a mental illness or tell the risk of getting a mental illness in the future.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nimh.nih.gov/health/publications/neuroimaging-and-mental-illness-a-window-into-the-brain/neuroimaging-and-mental-illness-a-window-into-the-brain.shtml|website=National Institute of Some clinicians are beginning to utilize [[genetics]]<ref name=Krebs>{{cite journal|vauthors=Krebs MO|title=Future contributions on genetics|journal=The World Journal of Biological Psychiatry|volume=6 |issue=Sup 2|pages=49–55|year=2005|pmid=16166024|doi=10.1080/15622970510030072|s2cid=44658585}}</ref><ref name=Benes>{{cite journal|vauthors=Hensch T, Herold U, Brocke B|title=An electrophysiological endophenotype of hypomanic and hyperthymic personality|journal=Journal of Affective Disorders|volume=101|issue=1–3|pages=13–26|date=August 2007|pmid=17207536|doi=10.1016/j.jad.2006.11.018}}</ref><ref name=Vonk>{{cite journal|vauthors=Vonk R, van der Schot AC, Kahn RS, Nolen WA, Drexhage HA|title=Is autoimmune thyroiditis part of the genetic vulnerability (or an endophenotype) for bipolar
