first-episode schizophrenia seems mediated by depression |journal=[[Comprehensive Psychiatry]] |volume=53 |issue=5 |pages=456–460 |doi=10.1016/j.comppsych.2011.07.005 |pmid=21871617}}</ref> predicting initial social dysfunction in people with either schizophrenic or bipolar psychosis;<ref name="haug2014">{{Cite journal |last1=Haug |first1=Elisabeth |last2=Øie |first2=Merete |last3=Andreassen |first3=Ole A. |last4=Bratlien |first4=Unni |last5=Raballo |first5=Andrea |last6=Nelson |first6=Barnaby |last7=Møller |first7=Paul |last8=Melle |first8=Ingrid  |date=April 2014 |title=Anomalous self-experiences contribute independently to social dysfunction in the early phases of schizophrenia and psychotic bipolar disorder |journal=[[Comprehensive Psychiatry]] |volume=55 |issue=3 |pages=475–482 |doi=10.1016/j.comppsych.2013.11.010 |pmid=24378241}}</ref> and whether a person will move to a schizophrenia spectrum diagnosis later.<ref name="parnas2016">{{Cite journal |author=[[Josef Parnas]], John Carter & Julie Nordgaard |date=February 2016 |title=Premorbid self-disorders and lifetime diagnosis in the schizophrenia spectrum: a prospective high-risk study |journal=[[Early Intervention in Psychiatry]] |volume=10 |issue=1 |pages=45–53 |doi=10.1111/eip.12140 |pmid=24725282 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

Considering the presence of self-disorders is useful when attempting to differentially diagnose disorders that can be confused with [[schizophrenia spectrum]] disorders. [[Autism spectrum disorder]] and [[schizotypal personality disorder]] can appear outwardly similar but have different etiologies and require different treatment approaches.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Nilsson |first1=Maria |last2=Handest |first2=Peter |last3=Nylander |first3=Lena |last4=Pedersen |first4=Lennart |last5=Carlsson |first5=Jessica |last6=Arnfred |first6=Sidse |date=2019 |title=Arguments for a Phenomenologically Informed Clinical Approach to Autism Spectrum Disorder |url=https://www.karger.com/Article/FullText/500294 |journal=Psychopathology |language=en |volume=52 |issue=3 |pages=153–160 |doi=10.1159/000500294 |issn=0254-4962 |pmid=31170725 |s2cid=174812132 |url-access=subscription |doi-access=free |archive-date=2023-04-27 |access-date=2023-04-27 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230427190320/https://www.karger.com/Article/FullText/500294 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Nilsson |first1=Maria |last2=Arnfred |first2=Sidse |last3=Carlsson |first3=Jessica |last4=Nylander |first4=Lena |last5=Pedersen |first5=Lennart |last6=Mortensen |first6=Erik Lykke |last7=Handest |first7=Peter |date=2020-01-04 |title=Self-Disorders in Asperger Syndrome Compared to Schizotypal Disorder: A Clinical Study |url=https://academic.oup.com/schizophreniabulletin/article/46/1/121/5485220 |journal=[[Schizophrenia Bulletin]] |language=en |volume=46 |issue=1 |pages=121–129 |doi=10.1093/schbul/sbz036 |issn=0586-7614 |pmc=6942161 |pmid=31050761 |archive-date=2023-08-07 |access-date=2023-08-07 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230807013936/https://academic.oup.com/schizophreniabulletin/article/46/1/121/5485220 |url-status=live }}</ref> The presence of self-disorders is evidence for a diagnosis of schizotypal personality disorder over autism spectrum disorder.<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Parvaiz |first1=Rizwan |last2=Vindbjerg |first2=Erik |last3=Crespi |first3=Bernard |last4=Happe |first4=Francesca |last5=Schalbroeck |first5=Rik |last6=Al-Sayegh |first6=Zainab |last7=Danielsen |first7=Ida-Marie |last8=Tonge |first8=Bruce |last9=Videbech |first9=Poul |last10=Abu-Akel |first10=Ahmad |date=2023-03-28 |title=Protocol for the development and testing of the schiZotypy Autism Questionnaire (ZAQ) in adults: a new screening tool to discriminate autism spectrum disorder from schizotypal disorder |journal=BMC Psychiatry |publisher=Springer Science and Business Media LLC |volume=23 |issue=1 |page=200 |doi=10.1186/s12888-023-04690-3 |issn=1471-244X |pmc=10044373 |pmid=36978026 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Likewise, in the case of first instance psychosis, self-disorders are indicative of a diagnosis of schizophrenia in favor of other psychotic disorders.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Spark |first1=Jessica |last2=Gawęda |first2=Łukasz |last3=Allott |first3=Kelly |last4=Hartmann |first4=Jessica A. |last5=Jack |first5=Bradley N. |last6=Koren |first6=Dan |last7=Lavoie |first7=Suzie |last8=Li |first8=Emily |last9=McGorry |first9=Patrick D. |last10=Parnas |first10=Josef |last11=Polari |first11=Andrea |last12=Sass |first12=Louis A. |last13=Whitford |first13=Thomas |last14=Nelson |first14=Barnaby |date=February 2021 |title=Distinguishing schizophrenia spectrum from non-spectrum disorders among young patients with first episode psychosis and at high clinical risk: The role of basic self-disturbance and neurocognition |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0920996420306526 |journal=Schizophrenia Research |language=en |volume=228 |pages=19–28 |doi=10.1016/j.schres.2020.11.061 |pmid=33434729 |s2cid=231201763 |url-access=subscription}}</ref>

The presence of self-disorders may cause reduced person insight into their illness through the alteration of the basic structures of consciousness.<ref name="parnasrev"/><ref name="henriksen2014"/>

Self-disorders are difficult for the people experiencing them to articulate spontaneously;<ref name="ease"/><ref name="schultze-lutterrev"/> and are not well-known, by either the general public or professionals in the field. Because of this, people will often make vague, clichéd complaints that mimic the symptoms of other mental disorders, symptoms such as "fatigue" or "concentration difficulties". Were a knowledgeable clinician to probe deeper, however, the underlying self-disorders may be assessed and help clarify the nature of the person's illness. In their review, Parnas, et al. (2014) say, "The psychiatrist's acquaintance with the phenomenon of 'non-specific specificity' is, in our view, extremely important in the context of early diagnostic assessment, especially of people presenting with a vague, unelaborated picture of [[adjustment disorder|maladjustment]], [[underperformance]], chronic [[malaise]] and [[dysphoria]], [[negative symptom]]s, or [[hypochondriasis|hypochondriac preoccupations]]." People with schizophrenia often describe their self-disorders as causing more suffering for them than psychosis.<ref name="parnasrev"/>

Self-disorders underlie most of the first-rank symptoms, those often termed passivity phenomena. There is a current proposal to list self-disorder as one of the symptoms of schizophrenia in the upcoming [[International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems|ICD-11]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Heinz |first1=A. |last2=Voss |first2=M. |last3=Lawrie |first3=S. M. |last4=Mishara |first4=A. |last5=Bauer |first5=M. |last6=Gallinat |first6=J. |last7=Juckel |first7=G. |last8=Lang |first8=U. |last9=Rapp |first9=M. |date=2016-07-15 |title=Shall we really say goodbye to first rank symptoms? |journal=European Psychiatry |volume=37 |pages=8–13 |doi=10.1016/j.eurpsy.2016.04.010 |issn=1778-3585 |pmid=27429167 |s2cid=13761854}}</ref>{{when|date=April 2025}}

== Evidence ==
The first systematic review of empirical studies on self-disorders based on the EASE scale was published in 2021. It found consistent support for the concept as a characteristic component of schizophrenia spectrum disorders and not other mental disorders.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Henriksen |first1=Mads Gram |last2=Raballo |first2=Andrea |last3=Nordgaard |first3=Julie |date=2021-11-08 |title=Self-disorders and psychopathology: a systematic review |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S2215036621000973 |journal=[[The Lancet Psychiatry]] |language=en |volume=8 |issue=11 |pages=1001–1012 |doi=10.1016/S2215-0366(21)00097-3 |pmid=34688345 |s2cid=239549566 |url-access=subscription |archive-date=2023-11-18 |access-date=2023-05-30 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231118090957/https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S2215036621000973 |url-status=live }}</ref> Another systematic review and meta-analysis from 2022 covering an aggregated sample of 810 patients found good evidence to support the existence of self-disorders as core clinical feature in schizophrenia spectrum disorders.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Burgin |first1=Sam |last2=Reniers |first2=Renate |last3=Humpston |first3=Clara |date=2022-01-21 |title=Prevalence and assessment of self-disorders in the schizophrenia spectrum: a systematic review and meta-analysis |journal=[[Scientific Reports]] |language=en |volume=12 |issue=1 |pages=1165 |bibcode=2022NatSR..12.1165B |doi=10.1038/s41598-022-05232-9 |issn=2045-2322 |pmc=8782935 |pmid=35064201 |doi-access=free}}</ref> The concept and its link to schizophrenia was likewise supported by a 2021 meta-analysis.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Raballo |first1=Andrea |last2=Poletti |first2=Michele |last3=Preti |first3=Antonio |last4=Parnas |first4=Josef |author-link4=Josef Parnas |date=2021-01-22 |title=The Self in the Spectrum: A Meta-analysis of the Evidence Linking Basic Self-Disorders and Schizophrenia |journal=[[Schizophrenia Bulletin]] |volume=47 |issue=4 |pages=1007–1017 |doi=10.1093/schbul/sbaa201 |pmc=8266610 |pmid=33479736 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Future directions and controversy ==
In a 2014 review, Postmes, et al., suggested that self-disorders and psychosis may arise from attempts to compensate for [[perceptual incoherence]] and proposed a hypothesis for how the interaction among these phenomena and the person's attempts to resolve the incoherence give rise to schizophrenia. The problems with the integration of sensory information create problems for the person in keeping a grip on the world, and since the self-world interaction is fundamentally linked to the basic sense of self, the latter is also disrupted as a result.<ref name="PostmesSno2014">{{cite journal |last1=Postmes |first1=L. |last2=Sno |first2=H.N. |last3=Goedhart |first3=S. |last4=van der Stel |first4=J. |last5=Heering |first5=H.D. |last6=de Haan |first6=L. |year=2014 |title=Schizophrenia as a self-disorder due to perceptual incoherence |journal=[[Schizophrenia Research]] |volume=152 |issue=1 |pages=41–50 |doi=10.1016/j.schres.2013.07.027 |issn=1573-2509 |pmid=23973319 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Sass and Borda have studied the correlates of the dimensions of self-disorders, namely ''disturbed grip'' (perplexity, difficulty "getting" stuff most people can get), ''hyperreflexivity'' (where thoughts, feelings, sensations, and objects pop up uncontrollably in the field of awareness, as well dysfunctional [[Human self-reflection|reflecting on matters and the self]]), and ''diminished self-affection'' (where the person has difficulty being "affected" by aspects of the self, experiencing those aspects as if they existed in an outer space), and have proposed how both primary and secondary factors may arise from dysfunctions in [[perceptual organization]] and [[multisensory integration]].<ref name="BordaSass2015">{{cite journal |last1=Borda |first1=Juan P. |last2=Sass |first2=Louis A. |year=2015 |title=Phenomenology and neurobiology of self disorder in schizophrenia: Primary factors |journal=[[Schizophrenia Research]] |volume=169 |issue=1–3 |pages=464–473 |doi=10.1016/j.schres.2015.09.024 |issn=1573-2509 |pmid=26516103 |s2cid=9844593}}</ref><ref name="SassBorda2015">{{cite journal |last1=Sass |first1=Louis A. |last2=Borda |first2=Juan P. |year=2015 |title=Phenomenology and neurobiology of self disorder in schizophrenia: Secondary factors |journal=[[Schizophrenia Research]] |volume=169 |issue=1–3 |pages=474–482 |doi=10.1016/j.schres.2015.09.025 |issn=1573-2509 |pmid=26603059 |s2cid=23648440}}</ref>

In a 2013 review, Mishara, et al., criticized the concept of the minimal self as an explanation for self-disorder, saying that it is unfalsifiable, and that self-disorder arises primarily from difficulty integrating different aspects of the self as well as having difficulty distinguishing self and other, as proposed by Lysaker and Lysaker: ''Ichstörung'' or ego disorder, as they say, in schizophrenia arises from disturbed relationships, and not from the "solipsistic" concept of the self as proposed by Sass, Parnas, and others.<ref name="MisharaLysaker2013">{{cite journal |last1=Mishara |first1=A. L. |last2=Lysaker |first2=P. H. |last3=Schwartz |first3=M. A. |year=2013 |title=Self-disturbances in Schizophrenia: History, Phenomenology, and Relevant Findings From Research on Metacognition |journal=Schizophrenia Bulletin |volume=40 |issue=1 |pages=5–12 |doi=10.1093/schbul/sbt169 |issn=0586-7614 |pmc=3885311 |pmid=24319117}}</ref> In his review, Sass agrees that the focus of research into self-disorder has focused too much on the self, and mentions attempts to look at disturbances in the person's relationship with other people and the world, with work being done to create an Examination of Anomalous World Experience, which will look at the person's anomalous experiences regarding time, space, persons, language, and atmosphere; he suggests there are problems with both the self and the world in people with self-disorder, and that it may be better conceptualized as a "presence-disturbance".<ref name="Sass2014">{{cite journal |last1=Sass |first1=Louis A. |year=2014 |title=Self-disturbance and schizophrenia: Structure, specificity, pathogenesis (Current issues, New directions) |journal=Schizophrenia Research |volume=152 |issue=1 |pages=5–11 |doi=10.1016/j.schres.2013.05.017 |issn=1573-2509 |pmid=23773296 |s2cid=17022508}}</ref> Parnas acknowledges the Lysaker model, but says that it is not incompatible with the concept of the minimal self, as they deal with different levels of self-hood.<ref name="parnasrev"/>

== History ==
The concept of a basic self-disturbance in schizophrenia appears in all the foundational texts on the disease.<ref name="parnasrev" /><ref name="andreasen2007" /> The [[basic symptoms of schizophrenia]] include descriptions of self-disorders.<ref name="ease" /> Likewise, [[Kurt Schneider]]'s first-rank symptoms, especially his concept of {{Interlanguage link|Ego disturbance|lt=ego disturbances|de|Ich-Störung}} as well as the so-called passivity phenomena may be considered as examples of self-disorders.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Nordgaard |first1=Julie |last2=Henriksen |first2=Mads Gram |last3=Berge |first3=Jonas |last4=Nilsson |first4=Lars Siersbæk |date=2019-08-01 |title=First-rank symptoms and self-disorders in schizophrenia |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0920996419302634 |journal=Schizophrenia Research |language=en |volume=210 |pages=306–307 |doi=10.1016/j.schres.2019.06.027 |issn=0920-9964 |pmid=31285076 |url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last=Bürgy |first=Martin |date=2011 |title=Ego Disturbances in the Sense of Kurt Schneider: Historical and Phenomenological Aspects |url=https://www.karger.com/Article/FullText/325059 |journal=Psychopathology |language=en |volume=44 |issue=5 |pages=320–328 |doi=10.1159/000325059 |issn=0254-4962 |pmid=21734435 |url-access=subscription |archive-date=2024-04-14 |access-date=2023-08-07 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240414003257/https://www.karger.com/Article/FullText/325059 |url-status=live }}</ref> Similar concepts were also discussed by [[Karl Jaspers]].<ref name=":3" /> The concept of "ontological insecurity", which resembles self-disorder, was proposed by [[R. D. Laing]] in 1960.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Nour |first1=Matthew M. |last2=Barrera |first2=Alvaro |date=November 2015 |title=Schizophrenia, Subjectivity, and Mindreading |url=https://academic.oup.com/schizophreniabulletin/article-lookup/doi/10.1093/schbul/sbv035 |journal=[[Schizophrenia Bulletin]] |language=en |volume=41 |issue=6 |pages=1214–1219 |doi=10.1093/schbul/sbv035 |issn=0586-7614 |pmc=4601706 |pmid=25848120 |archive-date=2024-06-05 |access-date=2023-08-17 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240605172909/https://academic.oup.com/schizophreniabulletin/article-lookup/doi/10.1093/schbul/sbv035 |url-status=live }}</ref>

The publication of the [[Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders#DSM-III (1980)|DSM-III (1980)]] lead to an increased emphasis on concrete signs and symptoms of mental disorders over the subjective experiences underlying those symptoms; in other words, it privileged a [[psychological behaviorism|behaviorist]] approach to diagnosis. Because the concept of self-disorders had been difficult to [[Operationalization|operationalize]], it began to be criticized as overly vague and too subjective; indeed, little systematic or empirical research was done on the concept in the 20th century. It therefore began to fall out of clinical use and soon disappeared entirely from training programs in the United States.<ref name="parnasrev" /><ref name="andreasen2007">{{Cite journal |author=[[Nancy C. Andreasen]] |date=January 2007 |title=DSM and the death of phenomenology in america: an example of unintended consequences |journal=[[Schizophrenia Bulletin]] |volume=33 |issue=1 |pages=108–112 |doi=10.1093/schbul/sbl054 |pmc=2632284 |pmid=17158191}}</ref><ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last1=Vollmer-Larsen |first1=Anne |last2=Handest |first2=Peter |last3=Parnas |first3=Josef |date=2007 |title=Reliability of Measuring Anomalous Experience: The Bonn Scale for the Assessment of Basic Symptoms |url=https://www.karger.com/Article/FullText/106311 |journal=Psychopathology |language=en |volume=40 |issue=5 |pages=345–348 |doi=10.1159/000106311 |issn=0254-4962 |pmid=17657133 |doi-access=free |archive-date=2023-11-28 |access-date=2023-08-07 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231128080221/https://www.karger.com/Article/FullText/106311 |url-status=live }}</ref>

A notable exception to this trend was the [[Bonn Scale for the Assessment of Basic Symptoms]] (BSABS), created in the 1980s to assess sub-clinical affective, cognitive and perceptual disturbances, as well as basic self-disturbance.<ref name=":4" /> In many studies, basic symptoms as measured by the BSABS were found to aggregate in people with schizophrenic and schizotypal disorders.<ref name="schultze-lutterrev">{{Cite journal |author=Frauke Schultze-Lutter |date=January 2009 |title=Subjective symptoms of schizophrenia in research and the clinic: the basic symptom concept |journal=[[Schizophrenia Bulletin]] |volume=35 |issue=1 |pages=5–8 |doi=10.1093/schbul/sbn139 |pmc=2643966 |pmid=19074497}}</ref>

In early 2000s, a group of researchers including Danish psychiatrist [[Josef Parnas]] sought to operationalize and revive the idea of schizophrenia as a disorder of the minimal self.<ref name=":3" /> This work resulted in the creation of the EASE, which was published in 2005.<ref name="ease" /><ref name="parnasrev" /> The scale was based on phenomenological interviews with first-admission people with schizophrenia spectrum disorders, to enable empirical research of self-disorders.<ref name="ease" /><ref name="parnasrev" /> It was also partially based on the BSABS, but more focused on items relating specifically to disturbed self-experience.<ref name=":3" /> The creation of the EASE resulted in an uptick in research into the topic, and the first [[systematic review]] of the concept was published in [[The Lancet Psychiatry]] in 2021, finding good empirical support for self-disorders as a defining characteristic of schizophrenia spectrum disorders.<ref name=":0" />
