A '''thought disorder''' ('''TD''') is a multifaceted construct that reflects abnormalities in [[Thought|thinking]], [[language]], and [[communication]].<ref name="Hart">{{cite journal | vauthors = Hart M, Lewine RR | title = Rethinking Thought Disorder | journal = Schizophrenia Bulletin | volume = 43 | issue = 3 | pages = 514–522 | date = May 2017 | pmid = 28204762 | pmc = 5464106 | doi = 10.1093/schbul/sbx003 }}</ref><ref name="Uzman2022">{{cite journal |vauthors=Uzman Özbek S, Alptekin K |title=Thought Disorder as a Neglected Dimension in Schizophrenia |journal=Alpha Psychiatry |volume=23 |issue=1 |pages=5–11 |date=January 2022 |pmid=36425242 |pmc=9674097 |doi=10.1530/alphapsychiatry.2021.21371 |doi-broken-date=11 August 2026 |url=}}</ref> Thought disorders encompass a range of thought and language  difficulties and include [[poverty of ideas]], perverted logic (illogical or delusional thoughts), [[word salad]], [[delusion]]s, [[Derailment (thought disorder)|derailment]],<ref name="APA5">{{cite APA Dictionary |title=Derailment |shortlink=derailment |access-date=23 February 2020 }}</ref> [[pressured speech]], [[poverty of speech]], [[tangentiality]], [[verbigeration]], and [[thought blocking]].<ref name="Roche"/> One of the first known  public presentations of a thought disorder, specifically [[obsessive–compulsive disorder]] (OCD) as it is now known, was in 1691, when Bishop John Moore gave a speech before Queen Mary II, about "[[religious melancholy]]".<ref>{{Cite web |title=The history of OCD {{!}} OCD-UK |url=https://www.ocduk.org/ocd/history-of-ocd/ |access-date=2023-05-12 |language=en-GB}}</ref>

Two subcategories of thought disorder are [[content-thought disorder]], and [[formal thought disorder]].<ref name="Uzman2022"/><ref name="APA1">{{cite APA Dictionary | title = Thought disorder | shortlink = thought-disorder | access-date= 23 February 2020 }}</ref> CTD has been defined as a thought disturbance characterized by multiple fragmented delusions. A formal thought disorder is a disruption of the form (or structure) of thought.<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1016/B978-1-4160-3370-7.00048-1 |chapter=Schizophrenia, Phobias, and Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder |title=Developmental-Behavioral Pediatrics |date=2009 |last1=Hardan |first1=Antonio Y. |last2=Gilbert |first2=Andrew R. |pages=474–482 |isbn=978-1-4160-3370-7 }}</ref><ref name="APA3">{{cite APA Dictionary |title=Formal thought disorder |shortlink=formal-thought-disorder |access-date=23 February 2020 }}</ref>
Also known as disorganized thinking, FTD affects the form (rather than the content) of thought.<ref name="Kircher1">{{cite journal | vauthors = Kircher T, Bröhl H, Meier F, Engelen J | title = Formal thought disorders: from phenomenology to neurobiology | journal = The Lancet. Psychiatry | volume = 5 | issue = 6 | pages = 515–526 | date = June 2018 | doi = 10.1016/S2215-0366(18)30059-2 |pmid = 29678679 | s2cid = 5036067 }}</ref><ref name="DSM-5"/> FTD results in disorganized speech and is recognized as a key feature of [[schizophrenia]] and other [[psychosis|psychotic disorders]]<ref name="APA4">{{cite APA Dictionary |title=Disorganized speech |shortlink=disorganized-speech |access-date=23 February 2020 }}</ref><ref name="DSM-5">{{cite book |title=Diagnostic and statistical manual of mental disorders : DSM-5. |date=2013 |publisher=American Psychiatric Association |isbn=9780890425541 |page=88 |edition=5th |url=https://archive.org/details/diagnosticstatis0005unse/page/88 }}</ref> (including [[mood disorder]]s, [[dementia]], [[mania]], and [[neurological diseases]]).<ref name="Saddock-thought disorder" /><ref name="APA4"/><ref name="Roche">{{cite journal | vauthors = Roche E, Creed L, MacMahon D, Brennan D, Clarke M | title = The Epidemiology and Associated Phenomenology of Formal Thought Disorder: A Systematic Review | journal = Schizophrenia Bulletin | volume = 41 | issue = 4 | pages = 951–62 | date = July 2015 | pmid = 25180313 | pmc = 4466171 | doi = 10.1093/schbul/sbu129 }}</ref> Unlike hallucinations and delusions, it is an observable, objective sign of psychosis.<ref name="Kircher1" /> FTD is a common core symptom of a psychotic disorder, and may be seen as a marker of severity and as an indicator of [[prognosis]].<ref name="Roche"/><ref name="Bora">{{cite journal | vauthors = Bora E, Yalincetin B, Akdede BB, Alptekin K | title = Neurocognitive and linguistic correlates of positive and negative formal thought disorder: A meta-analysis | journal = Schizophrenia Research | volume = 209 | pages = 2–11 | date = July 2019 | pmid = 31153670 | doi = 10.1016/j.schres.2019.05.025 | s2cid = 167221363 }}</ref> It reflects a cluster of cognitive, linguistic, and affective disturbances that have generated research interest in the fields of cognitive neuroscience, neurolinguistics, and psychiatry.<ref name="Roche"/>

[[Eugen Bleuler]], who named [[schizophrenia]], said that TD was its defining characteristic.<ref name="Colman">Colman, A. M. (2001) ''Oxford Dictionary of Psychology'', Oxford University Press. {{ISBN|0-19-860761-X}}</ref> Disturbances of thinking and speech, such as [[clanging]] or [[echolalia]], may also be present in [[Tourette syndrome]];<ref name="Barrera 2009">{{cite journal | vauthors = Barrera A, McKenna PJ, Berrios GE | title = Formal thought disorder, neuropsychology and insight in schizophrenia | journal = Psychopathology | volume = 42 | issue = 4 | pages = 264–9 | year = 2009 | pmid = 19521143 | doi = 10.1159/000224150 | s2cid = 26079338 }}</ref> other symptoms may be found in [[delirium]].<ref name="NobleGreene1996">{{cite book |last1=Noble |first1=John |title=Textbook of Primary Care Medicine |date=1996 |publisher=Mosby |isbn=978-0-8016-7841-7 |page=1325 }}</ref> A clinical difference exists between these two groups. Patients with psychoses are less likely to show awareness or concern about disordered thinking, and those with other disorders are aware and concerned about not being able to think clearly.<ref>{{cite book | vauthors = Jefferson JW, Moore DS |title=Handbook of medical psychiatry |url=https://archive.org/details/handbookofmedica0000moor |url-access=registration |publisher=Elsevier Mosby |year=2004 |isbn=0-323-02911-6 |page=[https://archive.org/details/handbookofmedica0000moor/page/131 131]}}</ref>

== <span class="anchor" id="Content-thought disorder"></span>Content-thought disorder ==

Thought content is the subject of a person's thoughts, or the types of ideas expressed.<ref name="Blitzstein-2022">{{Cite book |last1=Blitzstein |first1=Sean |title=First aid for the psychiatry clerkship |last2=Ganti |first2=Latha |last3=Kaufman |first3=Matthew S. |date=2022 |publisher=McGraw Hill |isbn=978-1-264-25784-3 |edition=6th |location=New York}}</ref> Mental health professionals define normal thought content as the absence of significant abnormalities, distortions, or harmful thoughts.<ref name="Snyderman-2009" /> Normal thought content aligns with reality, is appropriate to the situation, and does not cause significant distress or impair functioning.<ref name="Snyderman-2009">{{Cite journal |last1=Snyderman |first1=Danielle |last2=Rovner |first2=Barry |date=2009-10-15 |title=Mental status exam in primary care: a review |journal=American Family Physician |volume=80 |issue=8 |pages=809–814 |issn=1532-0650 |pmid=19835342}}</ref>

A person's cultural background must be considered when assessing thought content. Abnormalities in thought content differ across cultures.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=APA Work Group on Psychiatric Evaluation |date=January 2021 |title=The American Psychiatric Association Practice Guidelines for the Psychiatric Evaluation of Adults: Guideline V. Assessment of Cultural Factors |journal=Focus |language=en |volume=18 |issue=1 |pages=71–74 |doi=10.1176/appi.focus.18105 |pmid=32015730 |issn=1541-4094|pmc=6996070 }}</ref> Specific types of abnormal thought content can be features of different psychiatric illnesses.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Norris |first1=David R. |last2=Clark |first2=Molly S. |date=2021-04-01 |title=The Suicidal Patient: Evaluation and Management |journal=American Family Physician |volume=103 |issue=7 |pages=417–421 |issn=1532-0650 |pmid=33788523}}</ref>

Examples of disordered thought content include:

* [[Suicidal ideation]]: thoughts of ending one's own life.<ref name="McGraw Hill-2025">{{Cite book |title=Practical guide to history taking, physical exam, and functioning in the hospital and clinic |date=2025 |publisher=McGraw Hill |isbn=978-1-264-27803-9 |editor-last=Goldberg |editor-first=Charlie |series=Lange medical book |location=New York}}</ref>
* [[Homicidal ideation]]: thoughts of ending the life of another.<ref name="McGraw Hill-2025" />
* [[Delusion]]: A fixed, false belief that a person holds despite contrary undeniable & unfalsifiable evidence and that is not a shared cultural belief.<ref name="Blitzstein-2022" /><ref name="McGraw Hill-2025" />
* [[Paranoia|Paranoid ideation]]: thoughts, not severe enough to be considered delusions, involving excessive suspicion or the belief that one is being harassed, persecuted, or unfairly treated.<ref name="Wolters Kluwer-2020">{{Cite book |title=Pocket psychiatry |date=2020 |publisher=Wolters Kluwer |isbn=978-1-9751-1793-1 |editor-last=Puckett |editor-first=Judith A. |series=Pocket notebook |location=Philadelphia |editor-last2=Beach |editor-first2=Scott R. |editor-last3=Taylor |editor-first3=John B.}}</ref>

* Preoccupation: excessive and/or distressing thoughts that are stressor-related and associated with negative emotions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Eberle |first1=David J. |last2=Maercker |first2=Andreas |date=March 2022 |title=Preoccupation as psychopathological process and symptom in adjustment disorder: A scoping review |journal=Clinical Psychology & Psychotherapy |language=en |volume=29 |issue=2 |pages=455–468 |doi=10.1002/cpp.2657 |issn=1063-3995 |pmc=9291616 |pmid=34355464}}</ref> 
* [[Obsessive–compulsive disorder]]: As obsession, repeated [[intrusive thought]]s that are inappropriate, and distressing or upsetting, and [[compulsive behavior]] repeated actions as an attempt to rid the intrusive thoughts.<ref name="Blitzstein-2022" /><ref name="Wolters Kluwer-2020" />
* [[Magical thinking]]: A false belief in a causal link between actions and events. The mistaken belief that one's thoughts, words, or actions can cause or prevent an outcome in a way that violates the laws of cause and effect.<ref name="Wolters Kluwer-2020" /> 
* [[Idée_fixe_(psychology)|Overvalued ideas]]: false or exaggerated belief held with conviction, but without delusional intensity.
* [[Phobia|Phobias]]: irrational fears of objects or circumstances that are persistent.<ref name="Blitzstein-2022" />

* [[Poverty of ideas]]: abnormally few thoughts and ideas expressed.<ref name="Blitzstein-2022" />
* Overabundance of thought: abnormally many thoughts and ideas expressed.<ref name="Blitzstein-2022" />

==<span class="anchor" id="Overview"></span>Formal thought disorder==

Thought process is the form, flow, and coherence of [[thinking]].<ref name="Wolters Kluwer-2020" /> This is how language is used and ideas put together. A normal thought process is logical, linear, meaningful, and goal-directed that demonstrates rational, sequential connections between thoughts that allows others to understand.<ref name="Blitzstein-2022" /><ref name="Wolters Kluwer-2020" /> Thought process is not what a person thinks, rather it is how a person expresses their thoughts.<ref>{{Cite web |title=ADMSEP - Clinical Simulation Initiative eModules |url=https://www.admsep.org/csi-emodules.php?c=psych-interview&v=y |access-date=2025-01-14 |website=www.admsep.org}}</ref>

Formal thought disorder (FTD), also known as disorganized speech or disorganized thinking, is a disorder of a person's thought process in which they are unable to express their thoughts in a logical and linear fashion.<ref name="APA3"/> Mild forms of disorganised speech are quite common, and to be considered as a diagnostic criterion for psychosis it must be severe enough to prevent effective communication.<ref name="DSM-5"/> Disorganized speech is a core symptom of [[psychosis]], and therefore can be a feature of any condition that has a potential to cause psychosis, including [[schizophrenia]], [[mania]], [[major depressive disorder]], [[delirium]], [[postpartum psychosis]], [[Dementia|major neurocognitive disorder]], and [[Substance-induced psychosis|substance induced psychosis]].<ref name="Blitzstein-2022" /> FTD reflects a cluster of cognitive, linguistic, and affective disturbances, and has generated research interest from the fields of [[cognitive neuroscience]], [[neurolinguistics]], and [[psychiatry]].<ref name="Roche" />

It can be subdivided into clusters of positive and negative symptoms and objective (rather than subjective) symptoms.<ref name="Bora" /> On [[Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale|the scale of positive and negative symptoms]], they have been grouped into [[Scale for the Assessment of Positive Symptoms#Positive Formal Thought Disorder|positive formal thought disorder]] (posFTD) and [[Scale for the Assessment of Negative Symptoms#Items|negative formal thought disorder]] (negFTD).<ref name="Bora" /><ref name="Kircher1" /> Positive subtypes were [[pressure of speech]], [[tangentiality]], [[Derailment (thought disorder)|derailment]], incoherence, and [[illogicality]];<ref name="Bora" /> negative subtypes were [[poverty of speech]] and poverty of content.<ref name="Kircher1" /><ref name="Bora" /> The two groups were posited to be at either end of a spectrum of normal speech, but later studies showed them to be poorly correlated.<ref name="Kircher1" /> A comprehensive measure of FTD is the Thought and [[Language disorder|Language Disorder]] (TALD) Scale.<ref name="Kircher2">{{cite journal | vauthors = Kircher T, Krug A, Stratmann M, Ghazi S, Schales C, Frauenheim M, Turner L, Fährmann P, Hornig T, Katzev M, Grosvald M, Müller-Isberner R, Nagels A | display-authors = 6 | title = A rating scale for the assessment of objective and subjective formal Thought and Language Disorder (TALD) | journal = Schizophrenia Research | volume = 160 | issue = 1–3 | pages = 216–21 | date = December 2014 | pmid = 25458572 | doi = 10.1016/j.schres.2014.10.024 | doi-access = free | hdl = 10576/4730 | hdl-access = free }}</ref> The Kiddie Formal Thought Disorder Rating Scale (K-FTDS) can be used to assess the presence of formal thought disorder in children and their childhood.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Play diagnosis and assessment |date=2000 |publisher=Wiley |isbn=978-0-471-25457-7 |editor-last=Sandgrund |editor-first=Alice |edition=2nd |location=New York |editor-last2=Schaefer |editor-first2=Charles E.}}</ref> Although it is very extensive and time-consuming, its results are in great detail and reliable.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=de Bruin |first1=Esther I. |last2=Verheij |first2=Fop |last3=Wiegman |first3=Tamar |last4=Ferdinand |first4=Robert F. |title=Assessment of formal thought disorder: The relation between the Kiddie Formal Thought Disorder Rating Scale and clinical judgment |journal=Psychiatry Research |date=January 2007 |volume=149 |issue=1–3 |pages=239–246 |doi=10.1016/j.psychres.2006.01.018 |pmid=17156854 }}</ref>

[[Nancy Andreasen]] preferred to identify TDs as ''thought-language-communication disorders'' (TLC disorders).<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Andreasen |first=N. C. |date=1986-01-01 |title=Scale for the Assessment of Thought, Language, and Communication (TLC) |url=https://academic.oup.com/schizophreniabulletin/article-lookup/doi/10.1093/schbul/12.3.473 |journal=Schizophrenia Bulletin |language=en |volume=12 |issue=3 |pages=473–482 |doi=10.1093/schbul/12.3.473 |pmid=3764363 |issn=0586-7614}}</ref><ref name="AndreasenNC">{{cite journal | vauthors = Andreasen NC | title = Thought, language, and communication disorders. I. Clinical assessment, definition of terms, and evaluation of their reliability | journal = Archives of General Psychiatry | volume = 36 | issue = 12 | pages = 1315–21 | date = November 1979 | pmid = 496551 | doi = 10.1001/archpsyc.1979.01780120045006 }}</ref> Up to seven domains of FTD have been described on the Thought, Language, Communication (TLC) Scale, with most of the variance accounted for by two or three domains.<ref name="Kircher1" /> Some TLC disorders are more suggestive of severe disorder, and are listed with the first 11 items.<ref name="AndreasenNC" />

=== Diagnoses ===
In the diagnosis of a [[psychosis|psychotic disorder]], the [[DSM-5]] (as did DSM-4) uses the term ''disorganized thinking (speech)'' over formal thought disorder, used as a synonym. It was thought that formal thought disorder was too difficult to firmly define, and that inferences about a person's thinking can be gained from their speech.<ref name="Jerónimo">{{cite journal |vauthors=Jerónimo J, Queirós T, Cheniaux E, Telles-Correia D |title=Formal Thought Disorders-Historical Roots |journal=Front Psychiatry |volume=9 |issue= |article-number=572 |date=2018 |pmid=30473667 |pmc=6237835 |doi=10.3389/fpsyt.2018.00572 |doi-access=free |url=}}</ref><ref name="Jimeno">{{cite journal |vauthors=Jimeno N |title=Language and communication rehabilitation in patients with schizophrenia: A narrative review |journal=Heliyon |volume=10 |issue=2 |article-number=e24897 |date=January 2024 |pmid=38312547 |pmc=10835363 |doi=10.1016/j.heliyon.2024.e24897 |bibcode=2024Heliy..1024897J |doi-access=free |url=}}</ref> [[Clinical psychology|Clinical psychologists]] typically assess FTD by initiating an exploratory conversation with a client and  observing their verbal responses.<ref name="Hopkins">{{cite web |title=Thought Disorder {{!}} Johns Hopkins Psychiatry Guide |url=https://www.hopkinsguides.com/hopkins/view/Johns_Hopkins_Psychiatry_Guide/787025/all/Thought_Disorder#:~:text=In%20clinical%20practice%2C%20formal%20thought,are%20excluded%20from%20the%20diagnosis |website=www.hopkinsguides.com |language=en}}</ref>

FTD is often used to establish a diagnosis of [[schizophrenia]]; in [[Cross-sectional study|cross-sectional studies]], 27 to 80 percent of patients with schizophrenia present with FTD. A hallmark feature of schizophrenia, it is also widespread amongst other [[psychiatric disorders]]; up to 60 percent of those with [[schizoaffective disorder]] and 53 percent of those with [[Major depressive disorder|clinical depression]] demonstrate FTD, suggesting that it is not exclusive to schizophrenia. About six percent of healthy subjects exhibit a mild form of FTD.<ref name="Kircher1"/>  Less severe FTD may happen during the initial ([[prodromal]]) stage, and after psychosis has diminished.<ref name="DSM-5"/>

The characteristics of FTD vary amongst disorders. A number of studies indicate that FTD in [[mania]] is marked by irrelevant intrusions and pronounced combinatory thinking, usually with a playfulness and flippancy absent from patients with schizophrenia.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Holzman |first1=P. S. |last2=Shenton |first2=M. E. |last3=Solovay |first3=M. R. |title=Quality of Thought Disorder in Differential Diagnosis |journal=Schizophrenia Bulletin |date=January 1986 |volume=12 |issue=3 |pages=360–372 |doi=10.1093/schbul/12.3.360 |pmid=3764357 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Nestor |first1=Paul G. |last2=Shenton |first2=Martha E. |last3=Wible |first3=Cindy |last4=Hokama |first4=Hiroto |last5=O'Donnell |first5=Brian F. |last6=Law |first6=Susan |last7=McCarley |first7=Robert W. |title=A neuropsychological analysis of schizophrenic thought disorder |journal=Schizophrenia Research |date=February 1998 |volume=29 |issue=3 |pages=217–225 |doi=10.1016/S0920-9964(97)00101-1 |pmid=9516662 }}</ref><ref name="Solovay Comparative Studies of Thought">{{cite journal |last1=Solovay |first1=Margie R. |title=Comparative Studies of Thought Disorders: I. Mania and Schizophrenia |journal=Archives of General Psychiatry |date=January 1987 |volume=44 |issue=1 |pages=13–20 |doi=10.1001/archpsyc.1987.01800130015003 |pmid=3800579 }}</ref> The FTD present in patients with schizophrenia was characterized by disorganization, [[neologism]], and fluid thinking, and confusion with word-finding difficulty.<ref name="Solovay Comparative Studies of Thought"/>

There is limited data on the longitudinal course of FTD.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Yalincetin |first1=Berna |last2=Bora |first2=Emre |last3=Binbay |first3=Tolga |last4=Ulas |first4=Halis |last5=Akdede |first5=Berna Binnur |last6=Alptekin |first6=Koksal |title=Formal thought disorder in schizophrenia and bipolar disorder: A systematic review and meta-analysis |journal=Schizophrenia Research |date=July 2017 |volume=185 |pages=2–8 |doi=10.1016/j.schres.2016.12.015 |pmid=28017494 }}</ref> The most comprehensive [[longitudinal study]] of FTD by 2023 found a distinction in the longitudinal course of thought-disorder symptoms between schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders. The study also found an association between social, work and educational functioning before first hospitalization and the longitudinal course of FTD.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Marengo |first1=J. T. |last2=Harrow |first2=M. |title=Longitudinal Courses of Thought Disorder in Schizophrenia and Schizoaffective Disorder |journal=Schizophrenia Bulletin |date=January 1997 |volume=23 |issue=2 |pages=273–285 |doi=10.1093/schbul/23.2.273 |pmid=9165637 }}</ref>

=== <span class="anchor" id="type"></span><span class="anchor" id="Speculative causes"></span>Possible causes ===

Several theories have been developed to explain the causes of formal thought disorder. It has been proposed that FTD relates to [[neurocognition]] via [[semantic memory]].<ref name="Harvey-2017" /> [[Semantic network]] impairment in people with schizophrenia{{Em dash}}measured by the difference between fluency (e.g. the number of animals' names produced in 60 seconds) and phonological fluency (e.g. the number of words beginning with "F" produced in 60 seconds){{Em dash}}predicts the severity of formal thought disorder, suggesting that verbal information (through [[semantic priming]]) is unavailable.<ref name="Harvey-2017" /> Other [[hypotheses]] include [[working memory]] deficit (being confused about what has already been said in a conversation) and attentional focus.<ref name="Harvey-2017">{{cite book | veditors = Sadock VA, Sadock BJ, Ruiz P | year = 2017 | title = Kaplan & Sadock's Comprehensive Textbook of Psychiatry | edition = 10th | isbn = 978-1-4511-0047-1 | publisher = Wolters Kluwer | vauthors = Harvey PD, Keefe RS, Eesley CE | chapter = 12.10 Neurocognition in Schizophrenia | at = Relationship of neurocognitive impairment to schizophrenia symptoms, Formal Thought Disorder}}</ref>

FTD in schizophrenia has been found to be associated with structural and functional abnormalities in the language network, where structural studies have found bilateral [[grey matter]] deficits; deficits in the bilateral [[inferior frontal gyrus]], bilateral [[inferior parietal lobule]] and bilateral [[superior temporal gyrus]] are FTD [[Correlation|correlates]].<ref name="Kircher1"/> Other studies did not find an association between FTD and structural aberrations of the language network, however, and regions not included in the language network have been associated with FTD.<ref name="Kircher1"/> Future research is needed to clarify whether there is an association with FTD in schizophrenia and neural abnormalities in the language network.<ref name="Kircher1"/>

[[Neurotransmitter]] dysfunctions that might cause FTD have also been investigated. Studies have found that [[Glutamate (neurotransmitter)|glutamate]] dysfunction, due to a [[rarefaction]] of glutamatergic [[synapse]]s in the superior temporal gyrus in patients with schizophrenia, is a major cause of positive FTD.<ref name="Kircher1"/>

The [[heritability]] of FTD has been demonstrated in a number of family and twin studies. [[Imaging genetics]] studies, using a semantic verbal-fluency task performed by the participants during [[Functional magnetic resonance imaging|functional MRI]] scanning, revealed that [[allele]]s linked to glutamatergic transmission contribute to functional aberrations in typical language-related brain areas.<ref name="Kircher1"/> FTD is not solely [[genetically determined]], however; environmental influences, such as allusive thinking in parents during childhood, and environmental risk factors for schizophrenia (including childhood abuse, migration, [[social isolation]], and [[Cannabis (drug)|cannabis]] use) also contribute to the pathophysiology of FTD.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=de Sousa |first1=Paulo |last2=Spray |first2=Amy |last3=Sellwood |first3=William |last4=Bentall |first4=Richard P. |title='No man is an island'. Testing the specific role of social isolation in formal thought disorder |journal=Psychiatry Research |date=December 2015 |volume=230 |issue=2 |pages=304–313 |doi=10.1016/j.psychres.2015.09.010 |pmid=26384574 }}</ref>

The origins of FTD have been theorised from a [[Social learning theory|social-learning]] perspective. Singer and Wynne said that familial communication patterns play a key role in shaping the development of FTD; dysfunctional social interactions undermine a child's development of cohesive, stable mental representations of the world, increasing their risk of developing FTD.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Singer |first1=Margaret Thaler |last2=WYNNE |first2=LC |title=Thought Disorder and Family Relations of Schizophrenics: IV. Results and Implications |journal=Archives of General Psychiatry |date=February 1965 |volume=12 |issue=2 |pages=201–212 |doi=10.1001/archpsyc.1965.01720320089010 |pmid=14237630 }}</ref>

=== Treatments ===
[[Antipsychotic]] medication is often used to treat FTD. Although the vast majority of studies of the efficacy of antipsychotic treatment do not report effects on syndromes or symptoms, six older studies report the effects of antipsychotic treatment on FTD.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Cuesta |first1=Manuel J. |last2=Peralta |first2=Victor |last3=De Leon |first3=Jose |title=Schizophrenic syndromes associated with treatment response |journal=Progress in Neuro-Psychopharmacology and Biological Psychiatry |date=January 1994 |volume=18 |issue=1 |pages=87–99 |doi=10.1016/0278-5846(94)90026-4 |pmid=7906897 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=X |last2=Savage |first2=R |last3=Borisov |first3=A |last4=Rosenberg |first4=J |last5=Woolwine |first5=B |last6=Tucker |first6=M |last7=May |first7=R |last8=Feldman |first8=J |last9=Nemeroff |first9=C |last10=Miller |first10=A |title=Efficacy of risperidone versus olanzapine in patients with schizophrenia previously on chronic conventional antipsychotic therapy: A switch study |journal=Journal of Psychiatric Research |date=October 2006 |volume=40 |issue=7 |pages=669–676 |doi=10.1016/j.jpsychires.2006.03.008 |pmid=16762371 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Remberk |first1=Barbara |last2=Namysłowska |first2=Irena |last3=Rybakowski |first3=Filip |title=Cognition and communication dysfunctions in early-onset schizophrenia: Effect of risperidone |journal=Progress in Neuro-Psychopharmacology and Biological Psychiatry |date=December 2012 |volume=39 |issue=2 |pages=348–354 |doi=10.1016/j.pnpbp.2012.07.007 |pmid=22819848 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Namyslowska |first1=Irena |title=Thought disorders in schizophrenia before and after pharmacological treatment |journal=Comprehensive Psychiatry |date=January 1975 |volume=16 |issue=1 |pages=37–42 |doi=10.1016/0010-440X(75)90018-8 |pmid=1109833 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hurt |first1=Stephen W. |title=Thought Disorder: The Measurement of Its Changes |journal=Archives of General Psychiatry |date=December 1983 |volume=40 |issue=12 |pages=1281–1285 |doi=10.1001/archpsyc.1983.01790110023005 |pmid=6139992 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Spohn |first1=H. E. |last2=Coyne |first2=L. |last3=Larson |first3=J. |last4=Mittleman |first4=F. |last5=Spray |first5=J. |last6=Hayes |first6=K. |title=Episodic and Residual Thought Pathology in Chronic Schizophrenics: Effect of Neuroleptics |journal=Schizophrenia Bulletin |date=January 1986 |volume=12 |issue=3 |pages=394–407 |doi=10.1093/schbul/12.3.394 |pmid=2876514 }}</ref> These studies and clinical experience indicate that antipsychotics are often an effective treatment for patients with positive or negative FTD, but not all patients respond to them.

[[Cognitive behavioral therapy]] (CBT) is another treatment for FTD, but its effectiveness has not been well-studied.<ref name="Kircher1"/> Large [[Randomized controlled trial|randomised controlled trials]] evaluating the effectiveness of CBT for treating psychosis often exclude individuals with severe FTD because it reduces the [[therapeutic alliance]] required by the therapy.<ref name="Palmier-Claus Griffiths Murphy Cognitive behavioural therapy">{{cite journal |last1=Palmier-Claus |first1=Jasper |last2=Griffiths |first2=Robert |last3=Murphy |first3=Elizabeth |last4=Parker |first4=Sophie |last5=Longden |first5=Eleanor |last6=Bowe |first6=Samantha |last7=Steele |first7=Ann |last8=French |first8=Paul |last9=Morrison |first9=Anthony |last10=Tai |first10=Sara |title=Cognitive behavioural therapy for thought disorder in psychosis |journal=Psychosis |date=2 October 2017 |volume=9 |issue=4 |pages=347–357 |doi=10.1080/17522439.2017.1363276 |url=https://eprints.lancs.ac.uk/id/eprint/131759/2/ARC_PSYCHOSIS_FOR_SUBMISSION_CBT_FTD.pdf }}</ref> However, provisional evidence suggests that FTD may not preclude the effectiveness of CBT.<ref name="Palmier-Claus Griffiths Murphy Cognitive behavioural therapy"/>
Kircher and colleagues have suggested that the following methods should be used in CBT for patients with FTD:<ref name="Kircher1"/>
*Practice structuring, summarizing, and feedback methods
*Repeat and clarify the core issues and main emotions that the patient is trying to communicate
*Gently encourage patients to clarify what they are trying to communicate
*Ask patients to clearly state their communication goal
*Ask patients to slow down and explain how one point leads to another
*Help patients identify the links between ideas
*Identify the main affect linked to the thought disorder
*Normalize problems with thinking

== Signs and symptoms ==
Language abnormalities exist in the general population, and do not necessarily indicate a mental health condition.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Çokal |first1=Derya |last2=Sevilla |first2=Gabriel |last3=Jones |first3=William Stephen |last4=Zimmerer |first4=Vitor |last5=Deamer |first5=Felicity |last6=Douglas |first6=Maggie |last7=Spencer |first7=Helen |last8=Turkington |first8=Douglas |last9=Ferrier |first9=Nicol |last10=Varley |first10=Rosemary |last11=Watson |first11=Stuart |last12=Hinzen |first12=Wolfram |title=The language profile of formal thought disorder |journal=npj Schizophrenia |date=19 September 2018 |volume=4 |issue=1 |page=18 |doi=10.1038/s41537-018-0061-9  |doi-access=free|pmid=30232371 |pmc=6145886 }}</ref> They can also occur in schizophrenia and other disorders (such as [[mania]] or [[Depression (mood)|depression]]), or in anyone who may be [[Fatigue|tired]] or [[Psychological stress|stressed]].<ref name="Hart"/><ref name="Fatemi2016">{{Cite book |url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-1-4939-2528-5 |title=The Medical Basis of Psychiatry |publisher=Springer New York |year=2016 |isbn=978-1-4939-2527-8 |editor-last=Fatemi |editor-first=S. Hossein |edition=4th |pages=497–506 |language=en |chapter=25. Thought Disorder |doi=10.1007/978-1-4939-2528-5 |editor-last2=Clayton |editor-first2=Paula J.}}</ref> To distinguish thought disorder as a mental health condition, professionals may consider patterns of speech, the severity and frequency of symptoms, and any resulting functional impairment.<ref name="AndreasenNC"/>

Symptoms of FTD include [[Derailment (thought disorder)|derailment]],<ref name="APA5"/> [[pressured speech]], [[poverty of speech]], [[tangentiality]], and [[thought blocking]].<ref name="Roche"/> The most common forms of FTD observed are tangentiality and circumstantiality.<ref>{{Cite web |title=UpToDate |url=https://www.uptodate.com/contents/schizophrenia-in-adults-clinical-features-assessment-and-diagnosis |access-date=2025-01-14 |website=www.uptodate.com}}</ref> FTD is a hallmark feature of [[schizophrenia]], but is also associated with other conditions that can cause [[psychosis]] (including [[mood disorder]]s, [[dementia]], [[mania]], and [[neurological diseases]]).<ref name="APA3" /><ref name="Saddock-thought disorder" /><ref name="Fatemi2016" /> Impaired [[attention]], poor [[memory]], and difficulty formulating abstract [[concept]]s may also occur with TD, and can be observed and assessed with mental-status tests such as [[serial sevens]] or memory tests.<ref name="Fatemi2016" />

=== Types ===
Thirty symptoms (or features) of TD have been described, including:<ref name="Fatemi2016" /><ref name="Kircher1"/>
*[[Alogia]]: A poverty of speech in amount or content, it is classified as a negative symptom of schizophrenia. When further classifying symptoms, poverty of speech content (which means there is little meaningful content within a normal amount of speech) is a disorganization symptom.<ref name="alogia as a disorganization symptom">{{harvp | Phenomenology of Schizophrenia | 2017 | loc = THE SYMPTOMS OF SCHIZOPHRENIA, Categories of Negative Symptoms. }}
*"... In this way, alogia is conceived of as a 'negative thought disorder.' ..."
*"... The paucity of meaningful content in the presence of a normal amount of speech that is sometimes included in alogia is actually a disorganization of thought and not a negative symptom and is properly included in the disorganization cluster of symptoms. ..."</ref> Under [[Scale for the Assessment of Negative Symptoms|SANS]], thought blocking is considered a part of alogia, and so is increased latency in response.<ref name=Sadock2008-Table-6-5>{{harvp | Kaplan and Sadock's Concise Textbook of Clinical Psychiatry | 2008 | loc = "6 Psychiatric Rating Scales", Table 6–5 Scale for the Assessment of Negative Symptoms (SANS), p. 44. }}</ref>
*[[Circumstantial speech]] (also known as ''circumstantial thinking''):<ref name="Sadock2017-Table7.1-6">Houghtalen, Rory P; McIntyre, John S (2017). "7.1 Psychiatric Interview, History, and Mental Status Examination of the Adult Patient". In Sadock, Virginia A; Sadock, Benjamin J; Ruiz, Pedro (eds.). Kaplan & Sadock's Comprehensive Textbook of Psychiatry (10th ed.). Wolters Kluwer. HISTORY AND EXAMINATION, Thought Process/Form, Table 7.1–6. Examples of Disordered Thought Process/Form. {{ISBN|978-1-4511-0047-1}}. indicates and briefly defines the follow types: Clanging, Circumstantial, Derailment (loose associations), Flight of ideas, Incoherence (word salad), Neologism, Tangential, Thought blocking</ref> An inability to answer a question without providing excessive, unnecessary or irrelevant detail.<ref>{{cite book | vauthors = Videbeck S | year = 2017 | title = Psychiatric-Mental Health Nursing | edition = 7th | publisher = Wolters Kluwer | isbn = 9781496355911 | chapter = 8. Assessment | at = CONTENT OF THE ASSESSMENT, Thought Process and Content, p. 232. }}</ref> Circumstantial speech eventually reaches a relevant point, unlike in tangential speech.<ref name="Blitzstein-2022" /> A patient may answer the question "How have you been sleeping lately?" with "Oh, I go to bed early, so I can get plenty of rest. I like to listen to music or read before bed. Right now I'm reading a good mystery. Maybe I'll write a mystery someday. But it isn't helping, reading I mean. I have been getting only 2 or 3 hours of sleep at night."<ref>{{harvp | Videbeck |2017 | loc = Chapter 16 Schizophrenia, APPLICATION OF THE NURSING PROCESS, Thought Process and Content, p. 446. }}</ref>
*[[Clanging]]: instances in which ideas are related only by phonetics (similar or rhyming sounds) rather than actual meaning.<ref name="Blitzstein-2022" /><ref name="Videbeck">{{cite book |last=Videbeck |first=S |title=Psychiatric-Mental Health Nursing, 4th ed. |year=2008 |publisher=Wolters Kluwers Health, Lippincott Williams & Wilkins |location=Philadelphia}}</ref><ref name="Care">{{cite web |title=Thought disorder |url=https://www.thenationalcouncil.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/07/Disorganized-Symptoms-of-Psychosis-Slides.pdf |access-date=26 February 2020 |archive-date=26 February 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200226195008/https://www.thenationalcouncil.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/07/Disorganized-Symptoms-of-Psychosis-Slides.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> This may present as excessive rhyming or alliteration ("Many moldy mushrooms merge out of the mildewy mud on Mondays", or "I heard the bell. Well, hell, then I fell"). It is most commonly seen in the manic phase of [[bipolar disorder]], although it is also often observed in patients with schizophrenia and [[schizoaffective disorder]].
*[[Derailment (thought disorder)|Derailment]] (also known as ''loosening of associations'' and ''knight's move thinking''):<ref name="Blitzstein-2022" /><ref name="Sadock2017-Table7.1-6" /> Thought frequently moves from one idea to another with little to no apparent relation, with frequent interruptions in thought. It can appear in both speech and in writing.<ref name="APA5"/> Derailment is essentially equivalent to a loosening of associations. ("The next day when I'd be going out you know, I took control, like uh, I put bleach on my hair in California").<ref name="Fatemi2016" />
*Distractible speech: Response changing mid-speech in response to a nearby stimulus ("Then I left San Francisco and moved to&nbsp;... Where did you get that tie?")<ref name="Fatemi2016" /><ref name="APA8">{{cite APA Dictionary |title=Distractible speech |shortlink=distractible-speech |access-date=3 March 2020 }}</ref>
*[[Echolalia]]:<ref name=Sadock2008-Thought>{{harvp | Kaplan and Sadock's Concise Textbook of Clinical Psychiatry | 2008 | loc = "10 Schizophrenia", CLINICAL FEATURES, Thought, pp. 168–169.  }} 
* "Form of Thought. Disorders of the form of thought are objectively observable in patients' spoken and written language. The disorders include looseness of associations, derailment, incoherence, tangentiality, circumstantiality, neologisms, echolalia, verbigeration, word salad, and mutism."
* "Thought Process. ... Disorders of thought process include flight of ideas, thought blocking, impaired attention, poverty of thought content, poor abstraction abilities, perseveration, idiosyncratic associations (e.g., identical predicates and clang associations), overinclusion, and circumstantiality."
</ref> Echoing of another's speech,<ref name=Videbeck/> once or in repetition. This may involve repeating the last few words of another person's sentences,<ref name="Sadock2008-Thought" /> and is common on the [[autism spectrum]] and in [[Tourette syndrome]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ganos |first1=Christos |last2=Ogrzal |first2=Timo |last3=Schnitzler |first3=Alfons |last4=Münchau |first4=Alexander |title=The pathophysiology of echopraxia/echolalia: Relevance to Gilles De La Tourette syndrome |journal=Movement Disorders |date=September 2012 |volume=27 |issue=10 |pages=1222–1229 |doi=10.1002/mds.25103 |pmid=22807284 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |title=Handbook of autism and pervasive developmental disorders |volume=1: Diagnosis, development, neurobiology, and behavior|date=2005|publisher=John Wiley|author=Fred R. Volkmar |display-authors=etal |isbn=978-0-470-93934-5|edition=3rd |location=Hoboken, NJ|oclc=60394857}}{{pn|date=September 2024}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Duffy|first=Joseph R. |title=Motor speech disorders: substrates, differential diagnosis, and management|date=2013|isbn=978-0-323-07200-7|edition=Third |location=St. Louis, MO|oclc=819941855|pages=314–315}}</ref> 
*Evasion (also known as ''paralogia'' and ''perverted logic''): The next logical idea in a sequence is replaced with another idea closely related to it, but inappropriate to the current conversational context.<ref name="APA6">{{cite APA Dictionary |title=Evasion |shortlink=evasion |access-date=23 February 2020 }}</ref><ref>{{harvp | Kaplan & Sadock's Comprehensive Textbook of Psychiatry | 2017 | loc = Appendix B Glossary of Psychiatry and Psychology Terms. }} "''evasion'' ... consists of suppressing an idea that is next in a thought series and replacing it with another idea closely related to it. Also called paralogia; perverted logic."</ref>
*[[Flight of ideas]]:<ref name=Sadock2017-Table7.1-6 /> A form of FTD marked by abrupt leaps from one topic to another, possibly with discernible links between successive ideas which may be governed by similarities between subjects or by [[Rhyme|rhyming]], puns, wordplay, or even by innocuous environmental stimuli (such as the sound of birds chirping). It is most characteristic of the manic phase of bipolar disorder.<ref name=Videbeck />
*[[Illogicality]]:<ref name=K&S-Concise-2008-Table-6-6>{{harvp | Kaplan and Sadock's Concise Textbook of Clinical Psychiatry | 2008 | loc = "Chapter 6 Psychiatric Rating Scales", OTHER SCALES, Table 6–6 Scale for the Assessment of Positive Symptoms (SAPS), Positive formal thought disorder, p. 45 }} includes and defines Derailment, Tangentiality, Incoherence, Illogicality, Circumstantiality, Pressure of speech, Distractible speech, Clanging.</ref> Conclusions are reached which do not follow logically (non sequiturs or faulty inferences). "Do you think this will fit in the box?" is answered with, "Well of course; it's brown, isn't it?"
*Incoherence ([[word salad]]):<ref name=Sadock2017-Table7.1-6 /> Speech which is unintelligible because the individual words are real, but the manner in which they are strung together produces relative gibberish.<ref name=Videbeck/> The question "Why do people comb their hair?" elicits a response like "Because it makes a twirl in life, my box is broken help me blue elephant. Isn't lettuce brave? I like electrons, hello please!"
*[[Neologism]]s:<ref name=Sadock2017-Table7.1-6 /> Completely new words (or phrases) whose origins and meanings are usually unrecognizable ("I got so angry I picked up a dish and threw it at the geshinker").<ref name="Fatemi2016" /> These may also involve [[elision]]s of two words which are similar in meaning or sound.<ref>{{cite journal|author2-link=Martin Rossor | vauthors = Rohrer JD, Rossor MN, Warren JD | title = Neologistic jargon aphasia and agraphia in primary progressive aphasia | journal = Journal of the Neurological Sciences | volume = 277 | issue = 1–2 | pages = 155–9 | date = February 2009 | pmid = 19033077 | pmc = 2633035 | doi = 10.1016/j.jns.2008.10.014 }}</ref> Although neologisms may refer to words formed incorrectly whose origins are understandable (such as "headshoe" for "hat"), these can be more clearly referred to as word approximations.<ref>{{harvp | Kaplan and Sadock's Concise Textbook of Clinical Psychiatry | 2008 | loc = "Chapter 4 Signs and Symptoms in Psychiatry", GLOSSARY OF SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS, p. 29 }}</ref>
*Overinclusion:<ref name=Sadock2008-Thought /> The failure to eliminate ineffective, inappropriate, irrelevant, or extraneous details associated with a particular stimulus.<ref name="Akiskal2016-Speech and Thought">{{cite book | ref = {{harvid | The Mental Status Examination | 2016 }} | veditors = Fatemi SH, Clayton PJ | year = 2016 | title = The Medical Basis of Psychiatry | edition = 4th | location = New York | publisher = Springer Science+Business Media | isbn = 978-1-4939-2528-5 | doi = 10.1007/978-1-4939-2528-5 | vauthors = Akiskal HS | chapter = 1 The Mental Status Examination | at = 1.5.5. Speech and Thought., pp. 8–10 }}
* "This form of thought is most characteristic of mania and tends to be overinclusive, with difficulty in excluding irrelevant, extraneous details from the association."</ref><ref>{{harvp | APA dictionary of psychology |2015 | p = 751 }} ''overinclusion'' n. failure of an individual to eliminate ineffective or inappropriate responses associated with a particular stimulus.</ref>
*[[Perseveration]]:<ref name=Sadock2008-Thought /> Persistent repetition of words or ideas, even when another person tries to change the subject.<ref name=Videbeck/> ("It's great to be here in Nevada, Nevada, Nevada, Nevada, Nevada.") It may also involve repeatedly giving the same answer to different questions ("Is your name Mary?"  "Yes."  "Are you in the hospital?"  "Yes."  "Are you a table?"  "Yes"). Perseveration can include [[palilalia]] and [[logoclonia]], and may indicate an organic brain disease such as [[Parkinson's disease]].<ref name="Sadock2008-Thought" />
*Phonemic [[paraphasia]]: Mispronunciation or syllables produced out of sequence ("I slipped on the lice and broke my arm").<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kurowski |first1=Kathleen |last2=Blumstein |first2=Sheila E. |title=Phonetic basis of phonemic paraphasias in aphasia: Evidence for cascading activation |journal=Cortex |date=February 2016 |volume=75 |pages=193–203 |doi=10.1016/j.cortex.2015.12.005 |pmid=26808838 |pmc=4754157 }}</ref>
*[[Pressured speech]]:<ref name="APA9">{{cite APA Dictionary |title=Pressured speech |shortlink=pressured-speech |access-date=23 February 2020 }}</ref> Rapid speech without pauses, which is difficult for others to interrupt.
*[[Self-reference|Referential thinking]]: Viewing innocuous stimuli as having a specific meaning for the self<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Cicero |first1=David C. |last2=Kerns |first2=John G. |title=Unpleasant and pleasant referential thinking: Relations with self-processing, paranoia, and other schizotypal traits |journal=Journal of Research in Personality |date=April 2011 |volume=45 |issue=2 |pages=208–218 |doi=10.1016/j.jrp.2011.02.002 |pmid=26028792 |pmc=4447705 }}</ref> ("What's the time?" "It's 7 o'clock. That's my problem").
*Semantic paraphasia: Substitution of inappropriate words ("I slipped on the coat, on the ice I mean, and broke my book").<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Buckingham |first1=Hugh W. |last2=Rekart |first2=Deborah M. |title=Semantic paraphasia |journal=Journal of Communication Disorders |date=January 1979 |volume=12 |issue=3 |pages=197–209 |doi=10.1016/0021-9924(79)90041-8 |pmid=438359 }}</ref>
*[[Stilted speech]]:<ref name="Lewis2017-Thought Disorder"/> Speech characterized by words or phrases which are flowery, excessive, and pompous<ref name=Videbeck/> ("The attorney comported himself indecorously").
*[[Tangential speech]]: Wandering from the topic and never returning to it, failing to produce requested information in response to questions<ref name=Videbeck/><ref name="APA7">{{cite APA Dictionary |title=Tangential speech |shortlink=tangential-speech |access-date=23 February 2020 }}</ref> ("Where are you from?" "My dog is from England. They have good fish and chips there. Fish breathe through gills").
*[[Thought blocking]] (also known as ''deprivation of thought'' and ''obstructive thought''): An abrupt stop in the middle of a train of thought after which the subject may not be able to continue.<ref name="APA Blocking">{{cite APA Dictionary|title=Blocking|shortlink=blocking|access-date=23 February 2020}}</ref>
*[[Verbigeration]]:<ref name=K&S2017-Continuity>{{harvp | Clinical Manifestations of Psychiatric Disorders | 2017 | loc = THINKING DISTURBANCES, Continuity. }} "Word salad describes the stringing together of words that seem to have no logical association, and verbigeration describes the disappearance of understandable speech, replaced by strings of incoherent utterances."</ref> Meaningless, stereotyped repetition of words or phrases in place of understandable speech; seen in schizophrenia.<ref name=K&S2017-Continuity /><ref>{{harvp | Kaplan and Sadock's Concise Textbook of Clinical Psychiatry | 2008 | loc = "Chapter 4 Signs and Symptoms in Psychiatry", GLOSSARY OF SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS, p. 32 }}</ref>

==<span class="anchor" id="Use of term"></span>Terminology==
Psychiatric and psychological [[glossaries]] in 2015 and 2017 defined ''thought disorder'' as disturbed thinking or [[cognition]] which affects [[communication]], [[language]], or thought content including poverty of ideas, [[Glossary of psychiatry#neologism|neologisms]], paralogia, [[word salad]], and [[delusion]]s<ref name="Saddock-thought disorder">
{{harvp | Kaplan & Sadock's Comprehensive Textbook of Psychiatry | 2017 | loc = Appendix B: Glossary of Psychiatry and Psychology Terms. }} "'''thought disorder''' Any disturbance of thinking that affects language, communication, or thought content; the hallmark feature of schizophrenia. Manifestations range from simple blocking and mild circumstantiality to profound loosening of associations, incoherence, and delusions; characterized by a failure to follow semantic and syntactic rules that is inconsistent with the person's education, intelligence, or cultural background."</ref><ref name="APA2">{{cite APA Dictionary|title=Content-thought disorder|shortlink=content-thought-disorder|access-date=23 February 2020}}</ref> (disturbances of thought content and form), and suggested the more-specific terms content thought disorder (CTD) and formal thought disorder (FTD).<ref name="APA1" /> CTD was defined as a TD characterized by multiple fragmented delusions,<ref name=K&S-content-thought-disorder>
{{harvp | Kaplan & Sadock's Comprehensive Textbook of Psychiatry | 2017 | loc = "Appendix B: Glossary of Psychiatry and Psychology Terms" }} "''content thought disorder'' Disturbance in thinking in which a person exhibits delusions that may be multiple, fragmented, and bizarre."</ref><ref name=APA2/> and FTD was defined as a disturbance in the form or structure of thinking.<ref>{{harvp | Kaplan & Sadock's Comprehensive Textbook of Psychiatry | 2017 | loc = "Appendix B: Glossary of Psychiatry and Psychology Terms" }} "''formal thought disorder'' Disturbance in the form of thought rather than the content of thought; thinking characterized by loosened associations, neologisms, and illogical constructs; thought process is disordered, and the person is defined as psychotic. Characteristic of schizophrenia."</ref><ref name="APA3"/>

The 2013 [[DSM-5]] only used the term FTD, primarily as a [[synonym]] for disorganized thinking and speech.<ref name="DSM-5"/> This contrasts with the 1992 [[ICD-10]] (which only used the word "thought disorder", always accompanied with "delusion" and "hallucination")<ref name="ICD-10">{{cite web | date = 1992 | title = The ICD-10 Classification of Mental and Behavioural Disorders: Clinical descriptions and diagnostic guidelines (CDDG) | url =https://www.who.int/entity/classifications/icd/en/bluebook.pdf | publisher = [[World Health Organization]] | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20041017011412/http://www.who.int/classifications/icd/en/bluebook.pdf | archive-date = 2004-10-17 | url-status=live }}
* '''F06.2 Organic delusional [schizophrenia-like] disorder''', p.59: Features suggestive of schizophrenia, such as bizarre delusions, hallucinations, or thought disorder, may also be present. ... ''Diagnostic guidelines'' ... Hallucinations, thought disorder, or isolated catatonic phenomena may be present. ...
* '''F20.0 Paranoid schizophrenia''', p. 80: ... Thought disorder may be obvious in acute states, but if so it does not prevent the typical delusions or hallucinations from being described clearly. ...
* '''F20.1 Hebephrenic schizophrenia''', p. 81: ... In addition, disturbances of affect and volition, and thought disorder are usually prominent. Hallucinations and delusions may be present but are not usually prominent. ...
</ref> and a 2002 [[medical dictionary]] which generally defined thought disorders similarly to the psychiatric glossaries<ref>{{cite book | ref = {{harvid | The BMA Illustrated Medical Dictionary |  2002 }} | year = 2002 | title = The British Medical Association Illustrated Medical Dictionary | publisher = Dorling Kindersley | isbn = 0-7513-3383-2 | pages = 547 | quote = '''thought disorders''' Abnormalities in the structure or content of thought, as reflected in a person's speech, writing, or behaviour. ... }}</ref> and used the word in other entries as the ICD-10 did.<ref>{{harvp | The BMA Illustrated Medical Dictionary | 2002}}
* p. 470 '''psychosis''': ... Symptoms include delusions, hallucinations, thought disorders, loss of affect, mania, and depression. ...
* p. 499-500 '''schizophrenia''': ... The main symptoms are various forms of delusions such as those of persecution (which are typical of paranoid schizophrenia); hallucinations, which are usually auditory (hearing voices), but which may also be visual or tactile; and thought disorder, leading to impaired concentration and thought processes. ...</ref>

A 2017 psychiatric text describing thought disorder as a "disorganization syndrome" in the context of schizophrenia:
{{Blockquote| "Thought disorder" here refers to disorganization of the form of thought and not content. An older use of the term "thought disorder" included the phenomena of delusions and sometimes hallucinations, but this is confusing and ignores the clear differences in the relationships between symptoms that have become apparent over the past 30 years. Delusions and hallucinations should be identified as psychotic symptoms, and thought disorder should be taken to mean formal thought disorders or a disorder of verbal cognition.
| ''Phenomenology of Schizophrenia'' (2017), THE SYMPTOMS OF SCHIZOPHRENIA<ref name="Lewis2017-Thought Disorder">{{cite book | ref = {{harvid | Phenomenology of Schizophrenia | 2017 }} | vauthors = Lewis SF, Escalona R, Keith SJ | veditors = Sadock VA, Sadock BJ, Ruiz P | year = 2017 | title = Kaplan & Sadock's Comprehensive Textbook of Psychiatry | edition = 10th | isbn = 978-1-4511-0047-1 | publisher = Wolters Kluwer | chapter = 12.2 Phenomenology of Schizophrenia | at = THE SYMPTOMS OF SCHIZOPHRENIA, Disorganization, Thought Disorder. }}
* As quoted in the templated quote.
* "Thought disorder is the most studied form of the disorganization symptoms. It is referred to as "formal thought disorder," or "conceptual disorganization," or as the "disorganization factor" in various studies that examine cognition or subsyndromes in schizophrenia. ..."</ref> }}
The text said that some [[clinician]]s use the term "formal thought disorder" broadly, referring to abnormalities in thought form with psychotic cognitive signs or symptoms,<ref>{{cite book | ref = {{harvid | Clinical Manifestations of Psychiatric Disorders | 2017 }}  | vauthors = Matorin AA, Shah AA, Ruiz P | veditors = Sadock VA, Sadock BJ, Ruiz P | year = 2017 | title = Kaplan & Sadock's Comprehensive Textbook of Psychiatry | edition = 10th | isbn = 978-1-4511-0047-1 | publisher = Wolters Kluwer | chapter = 8 Clinical Manifestations of Psychiatric Disorders | at = THINKING DISTURBANCES, Flow and Form Disturbances. | quote = Although formal thought disorder typically refers to marked abnormalities in the form and flow or connectivity of thought, some clinicians use the term broadly to include any psychotic cognitive sign or symptom. }}</ref> and studies of cognition and subsyndromes in schizophrenia may refer to FTD as ''conceptual disorganization'' or ''disorganization factor''.<ref name="Lewis2017-Thought Disorder" />

Some disagree:
{{Blockquote| Unfortunately, "thought disorder" is often involved rather loosely to refer to both FTD and delusional content. For the sake of clarity, the unqualified use of the phrase "thought disorder" should be discarded from psychiatric communication. Even the designation "formal thought disorder" covers too wide a territory. It should always be made clear whether one is referring to derailment or loose associations, flight of ideas, or circumstantiality.| The Mental Status Examination, ''The Medical Basis of Psychiatry'' (2016)<ref>{{harvp | The Mental Status Examination | 2016 | loc = 1.6.2. Disturbances in Thinking., pp. 14–15. }}</ref>
}}

Additionally, over the years same types of thought disorders were named differently. For example, ''desultory thinking'', ''loosening of association'', ''knight’s move thinking'' and ''crowding of thought'' describe the same tendency to jump from one idea to another with little relation. Lack of precise definitions can lead to confusion among clinicians and patients.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Rule |first=Ashley |date=December 2005 |title=Ordered thoughts on thought disorder |journal=Psychiatric Bulletin |language=en |volume=29 |issue=12 |pages=462–464 |doi=10.1192/pb.29.12.462 |issn=0955-6036|doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Course, diagnosis, and prognosis==
It was believed that TD occurred only in schizophrenia, but later findings indicate that it may occur in other psychiatric conditions (including mania) and in people without mental illness.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Neural correlates of formal thought disorder: An activation likelihood estimation meta-analysis|year = 2017|doi=10.1002/hbm.23706|pmc=5685170|pmid=28653797|last1 = Wensing|first1 = T.|last2 = Cieslik|first2 = E. C.|last3 = Müller|first3 = V. I.|last4 = Hoffstaedter|first4 = F.|last5 = Eickhoff|first5 = S. B.|last6 = Nickl-Jockschat|first6 = T.|journal = Human Brain Mapping|volume = 38|issue = 10|pages = 4946–4965 | doi-access=free }}</ref> Not all people with schizophrenia have a TD; the condition is not [[Sensitivity and specificity|specific]] to the disease.<ref name="Fatemi2016" />

When defining thought-disorder subtypes and classifying them as positive or negative symptoms, [[Nancy Andreasen]] found that different subtypes of TD occur at different frequencies in those with mania, depression, and schizophrenia. People with mania have pressured speech as the most prominent symptom, and have rates of derailment, tangentiality, and incoherence as prominent as in those with schizophrenia. They are likelier to have pressured speech, distractibility, and circumstantiality.<ref name="Fatemi2016"/><ref name="Andreasen1979A">{{cite journal | vauthors = Andreasen NC | title = Thought, language, and communication disorders. II. Diagnostic significance | journal = Archives of General Psychiatry | volume = 36 | issue = 12 | pages = 1325–30 | date = November 1979 | pmid = 496552 | doi = 10.1001/archpsyc.1979.01780120055007 }}</ref><ref name="Andreasen1979B">{{cite journal | vauthors = Andreasen NC | title = Thought, language, and communication disorders. I. Clinical assessment, definition of terms, and evaluation of their reliability | journal = Archives of General Psychiatry | volume = 36 | issue = 12 | pages = 1315–21 | date = November 1979 | pmid = 496551 | doi = 10.1001/archpsyc.1979.01780120045006 }}</ref><ref name="Andreasen1984">{{cite book | vauthors = Andreasen NC, Hoffrnann RE, Grove WM | year = 1984 | title = Mapping abnormalities in language and cognition | location = New York | publisher = Guilford Press | pages = 199–226 }}</ref>
 
People with schizophrenia have more negative TD, including poverty of speech and poverty of content of speech, but also have relatively high rates of some positive TD.<ref name="Fatemi2016"/> Derailment, loss of goal, poverty of content of speech, tangentiality and illogicality are particularly characteristic of schizophrenia.<ref>{{cite book | vauthors = Oyebode F | year = 2015 | title = Sims' Symptoms in the Mind: Textbook of Descriptive Psychopathology | edition = 5th | publisher = Saunders Elsevier | isbn = 978-0-7020-5556-0 | chapter = 10 Disorder of Speech and Language | at = Schizophrenic Language Disorder, CLINICAL DESCRIPTION AND THOUGHT DISORDER, p. 167. }}</ref> People with depression have relatively-fewer TDs; the most prominent are poverty of speech, poverty of content of speech, and circumstantiality. Andreasen noted the diagnostic usefulness of dividing the symptoms into subtypes; negative TDs without full affective symptoms suggest schizophrenia.<ref name="Fatemi2016"/>

She also cited the prognostic value of negative-positive-symptom divisions. In manic patients, most TDs resolve six months after evaluation; this suggests that TDs in mania, although as severe as in schizophrenia, tend to improve.<ref name="Fatemi2016"/> In people with schizophrenia, however, negative TDs remain after six months and sometimes worsen;  positive TDs somewhat improve. A negative TD is a good predictor of some outcomes; patients with prominent negative TDs are worse in social functioning six months later.<ref name="Fatemi2016"/> More prominent negative symptoms generally suggest a worse outcome; however, some people may do well, respond to medication, and have normal brain function. Positive symptoms vary similarly.<ref name="Fatemi2016"/>

A prominent TD at illness onset suggests a worse prognosis, including:<ref name="Lewis2017-Thought Disorder" />{{Div col | colwidth = 30em}} 
* illness begins earlier
* increased risk of hospitalization
* decreased functional outcomes
* increased disability rates 
* increased inappropriate social behaviors{{Div col end}}
TD which is unresponsive to treatment predicts a worse illness course.<ref name="Lewis2017-Thought Disorder" /> In schizophrenia, TD severity tends to be more stable than hallucinations and delusions. Prominent TDs are more unlikely to diminish in middle age, compared with positive symptoms.<ref name="Lewis2017-Thought Disorder" /> Less-severe TD may occur during the [[prodromal]] and residual periods of schizophrenia.<ref name="DSM-5"/>  Treatment for thought disorder may include psychotherapy, such as cognitive behavior therapy (CBT), and psychotropic medications.<ref name="Hopkins"/>

The [[DSM-5]] includes delusions, hallucinations, disorganized thought process (formal thought disorder), and disorganized or abnormal motor behavior (including [[catatonia]]) as key symptoms of psychosis.<ref name="DSM-5" /> Schizophrenia-spectrum disorders such as schizoaffective disorder and schizophreniform disorder typically consist of prominent hallucinations, delusions and FTD; the latter presents as severely disorganized, bizarre, and catatonic behavior.<ref name="APA3" /><ref name="DSM-5" /> Psychotic disorders due to medical conditions and substance use typically consist of delusions and hallucinations.<ref name="DSM-5" /><ref name="Ivleva-2017" /> The rarer [[delusional disorder]] and shared psychotic disorder typically present with persistent delusions.<ref name="Ivleva-2017">{{cite book | veditors = Sadock VA, Sadock BJ, Ruiz P | year = 2017 | title = Kaplan & Sadock's Comprehensive Textbook of Psychiatry | edition = 10th | isbn = 978-1-4511-0047-1 | publisher = Wolters Kluwer | vauthors = Ivleva EI, Tamminga CA | chapter = 12.16 Psychosis as a Defining Dimension in Schizophrenia | at = DSM-5: AN UPDATED DEFINITION OF PSYCHOSIS}}</ref> FTDs are commonly found in schizophrenia and mood disorders, with poverty of speech content more common in schizophrenia.<ref>{{cite book | veditors = Sadock VA, Sadock BJ, Ruiz P | year = 2017 | title = Kaplan & Sadock's Comprehensive Textbook of Psychiatry | edition = 10th | isbn = 978-1-4511-0047-1 | publisher = Wolters Kluwer | vauthors = Akiskal HS | chapter = 13.4 Mood Disorders: Clinical Features | at = BIPOLAR DISORDERS, Bipolar I Disorder, Acute Mania.}}</ref>

Psychoses such as schizophrenia and [[bipolar mania]] are distinguishable from [[malingering]], when an individual fakes illness for other gains, by clinical presentations; malingerers feign thought content with no irregularities in form such as derailment or looseness of association.<ref name="Ninivaggi-2017" /> Negative symptoms, including alogia, may be absent, and chronic thought disorder is typically distressing.<ref name="Ninivaggi-2017">{{cite book | veditors = Sadock VA, Sadock BJ, Ruiz P | year = 2017 | title = Kaplan & Sadock's Comprehensive Textbook of Psychiatry | edition = 10th | isbn = 978-1-4511-0047-1 | publisher = Wolters Kluwer | vauthors = Ninivaggi FJ | chapter = 28.1 Malingering | at = CLINICAL PRESENTATIONS OF MALINGERING, Psychological Symptomatology: Clinical Presentations, Psychosis.}}</ref>

Autism spectrum disorders (ASD) whose diagnosis requires the onset of symptoms before three years of age can be distinguished from early-onset schizophrenia; schizophrenia under age 10 is extremely rare, and ASD patients do not display FTDs.<ref>{{cite book | veditors = Sadock VA, Sadock BJ, Ruiz P | year = 2017 | title = Kaplan & Sadock's Comprehensive Textbook of Psychiatry | edition = 10th | isbn = 978-1-4511-0047-1 | publisher = Wolters Kluwer | vauthors = Sikich L, Chandrasekhar T | chapter = 53 Early-Onset Psychotic Disorders | at = DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS, Autism Spectrum Disorders}}</ref> However, it has been suggested that individuals with ASD display language disturbances like those found in schizophrenia; a 2008 study found that children and adolescents with ASD showed significantly more illogical thinking and loose associations than control subjects.<ref name="Solomon-2008" /> The illogical thinking was related to cognitive functioning and executive control; the loose associations were related to communication symptoms and parent reports of stress and anxiety.<ref name="Solomon-2008">{{cite journal | vauthors = Solomon M, Ozonoff S, Carter C, Caplan R | title = Formal thought disorder and the autism spectrum: relationship with symptoms, executive control, and anxiety | journal = Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders | volume = 38 | issue = 8 | pages = 1474–84 | date = September 2008 | pmid = 18297385 | pmc = 5519298 | doi = 10.1007/s10803-007-0526-6 }}</ref>

[[Rorschach test]]s have been useful for assessing TD.<ref name="Hart" /> A series of inkblots are shown, and responses are analyzed to determine disturbances of thought.<ref name="Hart" /> The nature of the assessment offers insight into the cognitive processes of another, and how they respond to equivocal stimuli.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Rapaport |first1=David |last2=Schafer |first2=Roy |last3=Gill |first3=Merton Max |title=Diagnostic Psychological Testing: The Theory, Statistical Evaluation, and Diagnostic Application of a Battery of Tests |date=1946 |publisher=Year book publishers |oclc=426466259 }}{{pn|date=September 2024}}</ref> [[Hermann Rorschach]] developed this test to diagnose schizophrenia after realizing that people with schizophrenia gave drastically different interpretations of [[Klecksography|Klecksographie]] inkblots from others whose thought processes were considered normal,<ref>{{Cite news|date=2012-07-24|title=What's behind the Rorschach inkblot test?|language=en-GB|work=BBC News|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/magazine-18952667|access-date=2021-07-15}}</ref> and it has become one of the most widely used assessment tools for diagnosing TDs.<ref name="Hart" />

The Thought Disorder Index (TDI), also known as the Delta Index, was developed to help further determine the severity of TD in verbal responses.<ref name="Hart" /> TDI scores are primarily derived from verbally-expressed interpretations of the Rorschach test, but TDI can also be used with other verbal samples (including the [[Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale]]).<ref name="Hart" /> TDI has a twenty-three-category scoring index; each category scores the level of severity on a scale from 0 to 1, with .25 being mild and 1.00 being most severe (0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00).<ref name="Hart" />

==<span class="anchor" id="Criticisms"></span>Criticism==
{{see also|Linguistic prescription}}
TD has been criticized as being based on circular or incoherent definitions.<ref name="Bentall">[[Richard Bentall|Bentall, R.]] (2003) ''Madness explained: Psychosis and Human Nature''. London: Penguin Books Ltd. {{ISBN|0-7139-9249-2}}{{pn|date=September 2024}}</ref>{{Request quotation | date=February 2020}} Symptoms of TD are inferred from disordered speech, based on the assumption that disordered speech arises from disordered thought. Although TD is typically associated with psychosis, similar phenomena can appear in different disorders and leading to misdiagnosis.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Tufan |first1=Ali Evren |last2=Bilici |first2=Rabia |last3=Usta |first3=Genco |last4=Erdoğan |first4=Ayten |title=Mood disorder with mixed, psychotic features due to vitamin b12 deficiency in an adolescent: case report |journal=Child and Adolescent Psychiatry and Mental Health |date=December 2012 |volume=6 |issue=1 |page=25 |doi=10.1186/1753-2000-6-25 |pmid=22726236 |pmc=3404901 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

A criticism related to the separation of symptoms of schizophrenia into negative or positive symptoms, including TD, is that it oversimplifies the complexity of TD and its relationship to other positive symptoms.<ref name="Arndt-1991" /> [[Factor analysis]] has found that negative symptoms tend to correlate with one another, but positive symptoms tend to separate into two groups.<ref name="Arndt-1991">{{harvp | Thought Disorder | 2016 | loc = 25.6. Relationship Between Thought Disorders and Other Symptoms of Schizophrenia., pp. 503–504. }} ''cited''
*{{cite journal | vauthors = Arndt S, Alliger RJ, Andreasen NC | title = The distinction of positive and negative symptoms. The failure of a two-dimensional model | journal = The British Journal of Psychiatry | volume = 158 | pages = 317–22 | date = March 1991 | pmid = 2036528 | doi = 10.1192/bjp.158.3.317 | s2cid = 41383575 }}
*{{cite journal | vauthors = Bilder RM, Mukherjee S, Rieder RO, Pandurangi AK | title = Symptomatic and neuropsychological components of defect states | journal = Schizophrenia Bulletin | volume = 11 | issue = 3 | pages = 409–19 | year = 1985 | pmid = 4035304 | doi = 10.1093/schbul/11.3.409 | doi-access = free }}
*{{cite journal | vauthors = Liddle PF | title = The symptoms of chronic schizophrenia. A re-examination of the positive-negative dichotomy | journal = The British Journal of Psychiatry | volume = 151 | pages = 145–51 | date = August 1987 | pmid = 3690102 | doi = 10.1192/bjp.151.2.145 | s2cid = 15270392 }}
</ref> The three clusters became known as negative symptoms, psychotic symptoms, and disorganization symptoms.<ref name="Fatemi2016"/> Alogia, a TD traditionally classified as a negative symptom, can be separated into two types: poverty of speech content (a disorganization symptom) and poverty of speech, response latency, and thought blocking (negative symptoms).<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Miller DD, Arndt S, Andreasen NC | title = Alogia, attentional impairment, and inappropriate affect: their status in the dimensions of schizophrenia | journal = Comprehensive Psychiatry | volume = 34 | issue = 4 | pages = 221–6 | year = 2004 | pmid = 8348799 | doi = 10.1016/0010-440X(93)90002-L }}</ref>
Positive-negative-symptom diametrics, however, may enable a more accurate characterization of schizophrenia.<ref>{{harvp | Phenomenology of Schizophrenia | 2017 | loc = THE SYMPTOMS OF SCHIZOPHRENIA, Negative Symptoms.  }} "The two-syndrome concept as formulated by T. J. Crow was especially important in spurring research into the nature of negative symptoms&nbsp;... but this does not diminish the creative efforts that led to these scales or importance of these scales for research. In fact, it was only through careful analysis of the structure of symptoms in these scales that a more accurate characterization of the phenomenology of schizophrenia was possible."
</ref>

<!-- Definition and symptoms -->

'''Alzheimer's disease''' ('''AD''') is a [[neurodegenerative disease]] and is the most common cause of [[dementia]], accounting for around 60–70% of cases.<ref name="WHO2025">{{cite web |title=Dementia |url=https://www.who.int/en/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/dementia |website=www.who.int |access-date=24 July 2025 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="Simon2018p111" /> The most common early symptom is difficulty in [[short-term memory|remembering recent events]].<ref name="Knopman2021" /> As the disease advances, symptoms can include [[aphasia|problems with language]], [[Orientation (mental)|disorientation]] (including easily getting lost), [[mood swing]]s, [[Apathy|loss of motivation]], [[self-neglect]], and [[challenging behaviour|behavioral issues]].<ref name="WHO2023" /> As a person's condition declines, they often [[Solitude|withdraw from family and society]].<ref name="BMJ2009">{{cite journal | vauthors = Burns A, Iliffe S | title = Alzheimer's disease | journal = BMJ | volume = 338 | page = b158 | date = February 2009 | pmid = 19196745 | doi = 10.1136/bmj.b158 }}</ref> Gradually, bodily functions are lost, ultimately leading to death. The median life expectancy following [[Medical diagnosis|diagnosis]] of dementia is three to twelve years.<ref name="todd" /> Co-occurring movement disorder, also known as [[Extrapyramidal symptoms|extrapyramidal signs]], [[Relative risk|multiplies risk]] of death by 1.6.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Zheng |first1=Xiaoting |last2=Wang |first2=Shichan |last3=Huang |first3=Jingxuan |last4=Li |first4=Chunyu |last5=Shang |first5=Huifang |date=2024-04-10 |title=Predictors for survival in patients with Alzheimer's disease: a large comprehensive meta-analysis |journal=Translational Psychiatry |language=en |volume=14 |issue=1 |page=184 |doi=10.1038/s41398-024-02897-w  |doi-access=free|pmid=38600070 |pmc=11006915 |issn=2158-3188}}</ref>

<!-- Cause, diagnosis and prevention -->
The causes of Alzheimer's disease remain poorly understood.<ref name=BMJ2009/> There are many environmental and genetic [[risk factor]]s associated with its development. The strongest genetic risk factor is from an [[allele]] (genetic variant) of [[apolipoprotein E]], a protein involved in the [[Lipid metabolism|metabolism of fats]] in [[mammals]].<ref name=Long/><ref name=NIA2021>{{cite web |title=Study reveals how APOE4 gene may increase risk for dementia |url=https://www.nia.nih.gov/news/study-reveals-how-apoe4-gene-may-increase-risk-dementia |publisher=National Institute on Aging |date=16 March 2021 |access-date=17 March 2021 |archive-date=17 March 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210317180050/https://www.nia.nih.gov/news/study-reveals-how-apoe4-gene-may-increase-risk-dementia }}</ref> Other risk factors include a history of [[head injury]], [[clinical depression]], and [[high blood pressure]].<ref name=Knopman2021/> The progression of the disease is largely characterised by the accumulation of [[Proteinopathy|malformed protein deposits]] in the [[cerebral cortex]], called [[amyloid plaques]] and [[neurofibrillary tangles]]. These misfolded [[Protein aggregation|protein aggregates]] interfere with normal cell function, and over time lead to irreversible [[Neurodegenerative disease|degeneration of neurons]] and loss of [[Synapse|synaptic connections]] in the [[human brain|brain]].<ref name="NIA2023">{{cite web |title=Alzheimer's Disease Fact Sheet |url=https://www.nia.nih.gov/health/alzheimers-disease-fact-sheet |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220323200727/https://www.nia.nih.gov/health/alzheimers-disease-fact-sheet |archive-date=23 March 2022 |access-date=23 March 2022 |publisher=National Institute on Aging}}</ref> A probable diagnosis is based on the history of the illness and [[cognitive test]]ing, with [[medical imaging]] and [[blood test]]s to rule out other possible causes.<ref name=NICE2014Diag>{{cite web |title=Dementia diagnosis and assessment |publisher=National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) |url=http://pathways.nice.org.uk/pathways/dementia/dementia-diagnosis-and-assessment.pdf|access-date=30 November 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141205184403/http://pathways.nice.org.uk/pathways/dementia/dementia-diagnosis-and-assessment.pdf|archive-date=5 December 2014}}</ref><ref name="NICE2018">{{cite report | title=Dementia: assessment, management and support for people living with dementia and their carers | publisher=[[National Institute for Health and Care Excellence]] (NICE) | date=20 June 2018 | url=https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng97 | access-date=8 July 2023 | id=NG97 }}</ref> Initial symptoms are often mistaken for [[normal brain aging]].<ref name=BMJ2009/> [[Histopathology|Examination of brain tissue]] is the only way to definitively diagnose Alzheimer's, but [[neuroimaging]] techniques and fluid biomarkers have made it possible to diagnose probable Alzheimer's disease [[in vivo]].<ref name=Chapleau2022/>

<!-- Management -->
No known treatments can stop or reverse its progression, though some may temporarily improve symptoms.<ref name=WHO2023/> A [[healthy diet]], [[physical activity]], and [[social engagement]] are generally beneficial in aging, and may help in reducing the risk of cognitive decline and Alzheimer's.<ref name="NIA2023"/> Affected people become increasingly reliant on others for assistance, often placing a burden on [[Dementia caregiving|caregivers]].<ref name="Demirbas2023"/> The pressures can include social, psychological, physical, and economic elements.<ref name="Demirbas2023">{{Cite journal |last1=Demirbas |first1=Murat |last2=Hahn-Pedersen |first2=Julie H. |last3=Jørgensen |first3=Henrik L. |date=August 2023 |title=Comparison Between Burden of Care Partners of Individuals with Alzheimer's Disease Versus Individuals with Other Chronic Diseases |journal=Neurology and Therapy |volume=12 |issue=4 |pages=1051–1068 |doi=10.1007/s40120-023-00493-6 |pmc=10310688 |pmid=37222859}}</ref> Exercise programs may be beneficial with respect to [[activities of daily living]] and can potentially improve outcomes.<ref name=Forb2015>{{cite journal | vauthors = Forbes D, Forbes SC, Blake CM, Thiessen EJ, Forbes S | title = Exercise programs for people with dementia | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 132 | issue = 4 | article-number = CD006489 | date = April 2015 | pmid = 25874613 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD006489.pub4 | pmc = 9426996 | type = Submitted manuscript }}</ref> Behavioural problems or [[psychosis]] due to dementia are sometimes treated with [[antipsychotic]]s, but this has an increased risk of early death.<ref name="NICE2014">{{cite web  |title=Low-dose antipsychotics in people with dementia |publisher=National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) |url=https://www.nice.org.uk/advice/ktt7/resources/non-guidance-lowdose-antipsychotics-in-people-with-dementia-pdf|access-date=29 November 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141205183329/https://www.nice.org.uk/advice/ktt7/resources/non-guidance-lowdose-antipsychotics-in-people-with-dementia-pdf|archive-date=5 December 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=16 June 2008 |title=Information for Healthcare Professionals: Conventional Antipsychotics |publisher=US Food and Drug Administration |url=https://www.fda.gov/Drugs/DrugSafety/PostmarketDrugSafetyInformationforPatientsandProviders/ucm124830.htm|access-date=29 November 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141129015823/https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drugsafety/postmarketdrugsafetyinformationforpatientsandproviders/ucm124830.htm|archive-date=29 November 2014 }}</ref>

<!-- Epidemiology, history, society, and research-->
