WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Psychopathology
======================================================================

{{short description|Scientific study of mental disorders}}
{{hatnote group|{{for|the academic journal|Psychopathology (journal)}}{{Distinguish|Psychopathy}}}}
{{Use British English|date=September 2021}}

'''Psychopathology''' is the study of mental illness. It includes the signs and symptoms of all mental disorders. The field includes [[Abnormal psychology|abnormal cognition, maladaptive behavior, and experiences]] which differ according to [[social norm]]s. This discipline is an in-depth study of symptoms, behaviors, causes, course, development, categorization, treatments, strategies, and more.

[[Biological psychopathology]] is the study of the biological [[etiology]] of abnormal cognitions, behaviour and experiences. [[Child psychopathology]] is a specialization applied to children and adolescents.

==History==
Early explanations for [[mental illness]]es were influenced by religious belief and [[superstition]]. Psychological conditions that are now classified as mental disorders were initially attributed to possessions by evil spirits, demons, and the devil. This idea was widely accepted up until the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Loschen |first=E. L. |date=April 1974 |title=Psychiatry and religion: A variable history |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1007/bf01532755 |journal=Journal of Religion & Health |volume=13 |issue=2 |pages=137–141 |doi=10.1007/bf01532755 |pmid=24408386 |issn=0022-4197|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

The Greek physician [[Hippocrates]] was one of the first to reject the idea that mental disorders were the result of possession by demons or the devil, and instead looked to natural causes. He firmly believed the symptoms of mental disorders were due to diseases originating in the brain. Hippocrates suspected that these states of insanity were due to imbalances of fluids in the body. He identified four fluids in particular: blood, black bile, yellow bile, and phlegm.

Furthermore, not long after Hippocrates, the philosopher [[Plato]] argued that the mind, body, and spirit worked as a unit. Any imbalance brought to these compositions of the individual could bring distress or lack of harmony within the individual. This philosophical idea would remain in perspective until the seventeenth century. It was later challenged by Laing (1960) along with Laing and Esterson (1964) who noted that it was the family environment that led to the formation of adaptive strategies.

In the eighteenth century's [[Romantic Movement]], the idea that healthy parent-child relationships provided sanity became a prominent idea. Philosopher [[Jean-Jacques Rousseau]] introduced the notion that trauma in childhood could have negative implications later in adulthood.

In the 1600s and 1700s insane asylums started to be opened to house those with mental disorders.<ref>{{Cite web |title=National Library of Medicine - National Institutes of Health |url=https://www.nlm.nih.gov/ |access-date=2024-05-12 |website=www.nlm.nih.gov |archive-date=2024-01-17 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240117000000/https://www.nlm.nih.gov/ |url-status=live }}</ref> [[Lunatic asylum|Asylums]] were places where restraint techniques and treatments could be tested on patients who were confined. These were early precursors for psychiatric hospitals.
[[File:State insane asylum, Reno, Nevada.jpg|thumb|A state insane asylum in Nevada.]]

In 1875 the German book ''[[Textbook of Forensic Psychopathology]]'' was published, written by [[Richard von Krafft-Ebing]], which became a standard [[Psychiatry|psychiatric]] textbook for [[University|Universities]] across [[Germany]].<ref name=":3">{{Citation |last=Triarhou |first=Lazaros C. |chapter=Richard von Krafft-Ebing (1840–1902) |date=2022 |title=The Brain Masters of Vienna: Psychology and Neuroscience Pioneers around the Secession up to the Anschluss |pages=245–248 |editor-last=Triarhou |editor-first=Lazaros C. |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-13052-6_47 |access-date=2024-08-31 |place=Cham |publisher=Springer International Publishing |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-031-13052-6_47 |isbn=978-3-031-13052-6 |chapter-url-access=subscription |archive-date=2024-08-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240821201955/https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-13052-6_47 |url-status=live }}</ref>

The scientific discipline of psychopathology was founded by [[Karl Jaspers]] in 1913. It was referred to as "static understanding" and its purpose was to graphically recreate the "mental phenomenon" experienced by the client. A few years earlier, in 1899, the German book ''[[Lehrbuch der Psychopathologischen Untersuchungs-Methoden]]'' was published by [[Robert Sommer (psychiatrist)|Robert Sommer]].

===Psychoanalysis===
{{Main|Psychoanalysis}}

[[Sigmund Freud]] proposed a method for treating psychopathology through dialogue between a patient and a psychoanalyst. Talking therapy would originate from his ideas on the individual's experiences and the natural human efforts to make sense of the world and life.<ref name="AllPsych">{{cite web |last1=Heffner |first1=Christopher |name-list-style=vanc |title=Chapter 9: Section 1: Psychopathology |url=https://allpsych.com/psychology101/psychopathology/ |access-date=18 February 2015 |website=AllPsych.com |date=21 August 2014 |publisher=AllPsych |archive-date=19 February 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150219075529/http://allpsych.com/psychology101/psychopathology/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Evolutionary Perspectives ===
[[Evolutionary psychiatry]] argues that some psychiatric conditions might have persisted because they carried evolutionarily adaptive functions historically, or because of an [[evolutionary mismatch]] with modern environments.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Nesse |first=Randolph M. |date=2023 |title=Evolutionary psychiatry: foundations, progress and challenges |journal=World Psychiatry |language=en |volume=22 |issue=2 |pages=177–202 |doi=10.1002/wps.21072 |issn=2051-5545 |pmc=10168175 |pmid=37159362}}</ref>

==As the study of psychiatric disorders==

The study of psychopathology is interdisciplinary, with contributions coming from [[clinical psychology]], [[abnormal psychology]], [[social psychology]], and [[developmental psychology]], as well as neuropsychology and other psychology subdisciplines. Other related fields include [[psychiatry]], [[neuroscience]], [[criminology]], [[social work]], [[sociology]], [[epidemiology]], and [[statistics]].<ref name="A TEXT BOOK OF PSYCHOPATHOLOGY">{{cite book|last1=Shah|first1=Syed Ahmad|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=IIY4DwAAQBAJ&pg=PA9|title=A text book of psychopathology|last2=Mushtaq|first2=Shahnawaz|last3=Naseer|first3=Miss Naureen|last4=Ahmad|first4=Aijaz|last5=Sharma|first5=Gargi|last6=Kovur|first6=Harpreet|date=2017|publisher=RED'SHINE Publication. Pvt. Ltd|isbn=9789386483201|name-list-style=vanc}}</ref>

Psychopathology can be broadly separated into descriptive and explanatory. Descriptive psychopathology involves categorising, defining and understanding symptoms as reported by people and observed through their behaviour, which are then assessed according to a social norm. Explanatory psychopathology looks to find explanations for certain kinds of symptoms according to theoretical models such as [[psychodynamics]], [[cognitive behavioral therapy|cognitive behavioural therapy]] or through understanding how they have been constructed by drawing upon Constructivist Grounded Theory (Charmaz, 2016) or Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis (Smith, Flowers & Larkin, 2013).<ref name="Sims">{{Cite book|last=Oyebode|first=Femi|title=Sims' Symptoms in the Mind: Textbook of Descriptive Psychopathology|publisher=Saunders/Elsevier|year=2015|isbn=978-0-7020-5556-0|edition=Fifth|location=Edinburgh; New York|page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=lnVYBAAAQBAJ&pg=PA4 4]|oclc=878098854}}</ref>

There are several ways to characterise the presence of psychopathology in an individual as a whole. One strategy is to assess a person along four dimensions: deviance, distress, dysfunction, and danger, known collectively as the four Ds. Another conceptualisation, the p factor, sees psychopathology as a general, overarching construct that influences psychiatric symptoms.

==Mental disorders==
Mental disorders are defined by a set of characteristic features, more than just one symptom. In order to be classified for diagnosis, the symptoms cannot represent an expected response to a common stress or loss that is related to an event. Syndromes are a set of simultaneous symptoms that represent a disorder.  Common mental health disorders include [[Depression (mood)|depression]],{{Clarify|date=May 2025}} [[generalized anxiety disorder]] (GAD), [[panic disorder]], [[phobias]], [[social anxiety disorder]], [[obsessive-compulsive disorder]] (OCD), and [[post-traumatic stress disorder]] (PTSD).<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sarrami Foroushani |first=Pooria |date=2013-01-17 |title=Computerised cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) for common mental disorders |doi=10.1186/isrctn24529487 |doi-access=free |url=https://www.isrctn.com/ISRCTN24529487 }}</ref> “A mental disorder is a syndrome characterized by clinically significant disturbance in an individual’s cognition, emotion regulation, or behavior that reflects a dysfunction in the psychological, biological, or developmental processes underlying mental functioning.”<ref name="DSM5Book">{{cite book |last1=American Psychiatric Association |title=Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders |date=2013 |doi=10.1176/appi.books.9780890425596 |isbn=978-0-89042-555-8 |url=https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/depression |ref=Yes }}</ref> 

Depression is one of the most common and most debilitating mental disorders worldwide.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Yael |first1=Levin |last2=Gerard |first2=Sanacora |title= Textbook of men's mental health |chapter-url=https://psycnet.apa.org/record/2006-20936-005 |chapter=Depression |date=2007 }}</ref> It affects how individuals think, feel, and act. Symptoms vary depending on each individual person and include feeling sad, irritable, hopeless, or [[Anhedonia|losing interest in activities once enjoyed]].

Generalized anxiety disorder is feeling worried or nervous more frequently than what correlates to real-life stressors.  It is more common in women than men and includes symptoms such as having trouble controlling worries, feelings of nervousness or restlessness, and difficulty relaxing.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Generalized Anxiety Disorder: When Worry Gets Out of Control - National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) |url=https://www.nimh.nih.gov/health/publications/generalized-anxiety-disorder-gad |access-date=2024-05-12 |website=www.nimh.nih.gov |language=en}}</ref>

Across large populations, women show higher diagnosed prevalence of internalizing mental disorders, while men show higher prevalence of externalizing disorders and higher rates of suicide mortality. These differences reflect biological factors, differential exposure to stressors, and gendered patterns of diagnosis and help-seeking.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Boyd |first1=Anders |last2=Van de Velde |first2=Sarah |last3=Vilagut |first3=Gemma |last4=de Graaf |first4=Ron |last5=O'Neill |first5=Siobhan |last6=Florescu |first6=Silvia |last7=Alonso |first7=Jordi |last8=Kovess-Masfety |first8=Vivane |last9=EU-WMH Investigators |date=2015-03-01 |title=Gender differences in mental disorders and suicidality in Europe: results from a large cross-sectional population-based study |journal=Journal of Affective Disorders |volume=173 |pages=245–254 |doi=10.1016/j.jad.2014.11.002 |issn=1573-2517 |pmid=25462424}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Meng |first1=Xiangfei |last2=D'Arcy |first2=Carl |date=2016-11-15 |title=Gender moderates the relationship between childhood abuse and internalizing and substance use disorders later in life: a cross-sectional analysis |journal=BMC Psychiatry |volume=16 |issue=1 |pages=401 |doi=10.1186/s12888-016-1071-7  |doi-access=free|issn=1471-244X |pmc=5111209 |pmid=27846829}}</ref>

==The four Ds==
A description of the four Ds when defining abnormality:

# ''[[Deviance (sociology)|Deviance]]'' is variation from statistical norms that result in a conflict with society. This term describes the idea that specific thoughts, behaviors and emotions are considered deviant when they are unacceptable or not common in society. Clinicians must, however, remember that minority groups are not always deemed deviant just because they may not have anything in common with other groups. Therefore, an individual's actions are defined as deviant when their behaviour is deemed unacceptable by the culture they belong to. However, many disorders have a relation between patterns of deviance and therefore need to be evaluated in a differential diagnostic model.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Singhai |first1=Kartik |last2=Suthar |first2=Navratan |last3=Gehlawat |first3=Pratibha |date=May 2020 |title=The 3 Ds of geriatric psychiatry: A case report |journal=Journal of Family Medicine and Primary Care |language=en-US |volume=9 |issue=5 |pages=2509–2510 |doi=10.4103/jfmpc.jfmpc_221_20 |doi-access=free |pmid=32754531 |issn=2249-4863|pmc=7380787 }}</ref>
# ''[[Distress (medicine)|Distress]]'' has to do with the discomfort that is experienced by the person with the disorder. This term accounts for negative feelings by the individual with the disorder. They may feel deeply troubled and affected by their illness. Behaviors and feelings that cause distress to individuals or to others around them are considered abnormal if the condition is upsetting to the person experiencing it. Distress is related to dysfunction in that it can be a useful asset in accurately perceiving dysfunction in an individual's life. However, these two are not always related because an individual can be highly dysfunctional while at the same time experiencing minimal [[Stress (biology)|stress]]. The important characteristics of distress are the upsetting events themselves and the way one responds to them.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Oltmanns |first=T.F. |date=2021-07-14 |title=Abnormal Psychology |edition=9th |publisher=Pearson |isbn=9780137554737}}</ref>
# ''[[Abnormality (behavior)|Dysfunction]]'' involves maladaptive behavior that impairs the individual's ability to perform normal daily functions. It includes dysfunction in the psychological, biological, or developmental processes that are associated with mental functioning.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Berenbaum |first1=Howard |last2=Oltmanns |first2=Thomas F. |date=February 1992 |title=Emotional experience and expression in schizophrenia and depression. |journal=Journal of Abnormal Psychology |language=en |volume=101 |issue=1 |pages=37–44 |doi=10.1037/0021-843X.101.1.37 |pmid=1537971 |pmc=4370316 |issn=1939-1846}}</ref> This maladaptive behavior has to be significant enough to be considered a diagnosis. It is recommended to look for dysfunction across an individual's life experience because there is a chance the dysfunction may appear in clear observable view and in places where it is less likely to appear.<ref name=":0" /> Such maladaptive behaviours prevent the individual from living a normal, healthy lifestyle. However, dysfunctional behaviour is not always caused by a disorder; it may be voluntary, such as engaging in a hunger strike.
# ''[[Violence|Duration]]'' is useful for clinicians as a criterion for diagnosis. Most symptoms have a specific duration that they must meet before being diagnosed. However, this can be harmful as not every person's experience is the same.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Telles-Correia |first=Diogo |date=October 2018 |title=Mental disorder: Are we moving away from distress and disability? |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jep.12871 |journal=Journal of Evaluation in Clinical Practice |language=en |volume=24 |issue=5 |pages=973–977 |doi=10.1111/jep.12871 |pmid=29327512 |issn=1356-1294|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

===The p factor===
[[Benjamin Lahey]] and colleagues first proposed a general "psychopathology factor" in 2012,<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Lahey BB, Applegate B, Hakes JK, Zald DH, Hariri AR, Rathouz PJ|date=November 2012|title=Is there a general factor of prevalent psychopathology during adulthood?|journal=Journal of Abnormal Psychology|volume=121|issue=4|pages=971–7|doi=10.1037/a0028355|pmc=4134439|pmid=22845652}}</ref> or simply "p factor". This construct shares its conceptual similarity with the [[G factor (psychometrics)|g factor of general intelligence]]. Instead of conceptualising psychopathology as consisting of several discrete categories of mental disorders, the p factor is dimensional and influences whether psychiatric symptoms in general are present or absent. The symptoms that are present then combine to form several distinct diagnoses. The p factor is modelled in the [[Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology]]. Although researchers initially conceived a three-factor explanation for psychopathology generally, a subsequent study provided more evidence for a single factor that is sequentially [[Comorbidity|comorbid]], [[Chronic condition|recurrent/chronic]], and exists on a continuum of severity and chronicity.<ref name="Caspi2014">{{cite journal | vauthors = Caspi A, Houts RM, Belsky DW, Goldman-Mellor SJ, Harrington H, Israel S, Meier MH, Ramrakha S, Shalev I, Poulton R, Moffitt TE | display-authors = 6 | title = The p Factor: One General Psychopathology Factor in the Structure of Psychiatric Disorders? | journal = Clinical Psychological Science | volume = 2 | issue = 2 | pages = 119–137 | date = March 2014 | pmid = 25360393 | pmc = 4209412 | doi = 10.1177/2167702613497473}}</ref>

Higher scores on the p factor dimension have been found to be correlated with higher levels of functional impairment, greater incidence of problems in developmental history, and more diminished early-life brain function. In addition, those with higher levels of the p factor are more likely to have inherited a [[genetic predisposition]] to mental illness. The existence of the p factor may explain why it has been "... challenging to find causes, consequences, biomarkers, and treatments with specificity to individual mental disorders."<ref name=Caspi2014 />

A 2020 review of the p factor found that many studies support its validity and that it is generally stable throughout one's life. A high p factor is associated with many adverse effects, including poor academic performance, impulsivity, criminality, suicidality, reduced foetal growth, lower [[Executive functions|executive functioning]], and a greater number of psychiatric diagnoses. A partial genetic basis for the p factor has also been supported.<ref name="clinpsy-071119-115848">{{Cite journal|last1=Smith|first1=Gregory T.|last2=Atkinson|first2=Emily A.|last3=Davis|first3=Heather A.|last4=Riley|first4=Elizabeth N.|last5=Oltmanns|first5=Joshua R.|date=2020-05-07|title=The General Factor of Psychopathology|url=https://www.annualreviews.org/doi/10.1146/annurev-clinpsy-071119-115848|journal=Annual Review of Clinical Psychology|language=en|volume=16|issue=1|pages=75–98|doi=10.1146/annurev-clinpsy-071119-115848|pmid=32040926 |s2cid=211078278 |issn=1548-5943|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

Alternatively, the p factor has also been interpreted{{By whom|date=May 2025}} as an index of general impairment rather than being a specific index that causes psychopathology.<ref name="clinpsy-071119-115848" />

==As mental symptoms==
The term psychopathology may also be used to denote behaviours or experiences which are indicative of mental illness, even if they do not constitute a formal diagnosis. For example, the presence of [[hallucination]]s may be considered as a psychopathological sign, even if there are not enough symptoms present to fulfil the criteria for one of the disorders listed in the [[Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders|DSM]] or [[International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems|ICD]].

In a more general sense, any behaviour or experience which causes impairment, distress or [[disability]], particularly if it is thought to arise from a functional breakdown in either the cognitive or neurocognitive systems in the brain, may be classified as psychopathology. It remains unclear how strong the distinction between maladaptive traits and mental disorders actually is,<ref name="NeuroticismMA">{{cite journal | vauthors = Jeronimus BF, Kotov R, Riese H, Ormel J | title = Neuroticism's prospective association with mental disorders halves after adjustment for baseline symptoms and psychiatric history, but the adjusted association hardly decays with time: a meta-analysis on 59 longitudinal/prospective studies with 443 313 participants | journal = Psychological Medicine | volume = 46 | issue = 14 | pages = 2883–2906 | date = October 2016 | pmid = 27523506 | doi = 10.1017/S0033291716001653 | s2cid = 23548727 | url = https://zenodo.org/record/895885 | archive-date = 2019-07-24 | access-date = 2019-06-30 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20190724213253/https://zenodo.org/record/895885 | url-status = live }}</ref><ref name="Ormel2014">{{cite journal|vauthors = Ormel J, Laceulle OM, Jeronimus BF |year=2014|title= Why Personality and Psychopathology Are Correlated: A Developmental Perspective Is a First Step but More Is Needed|journal= European Journal of Personality|volume=28|issue=4|pages=396–98|doi=10.1002/per.1971|s2cid=210187913}}</ref> e.g. [[neuroticism]] is often described as the personal level of minor psychiatric symptoms.<ref name="Ormel2013">{{cite journal | vauthors = Ormel J, Jeronimus BF, Kotov R, Riese H, Bos EH, Hankin B, Rosmalen JG, Oldehinkel AJ | title = Neuroticism and common mental disorders: meaning and utility of a complex relationship | journal = Clinical Psychology Review | volume = 33 | issue = 5 | pages = 686–697 | date = July 2013 | pmid = 23702592 | pmc = 4382368 | doi = 10.1016/j.cpr.2013.04.003}}</ref>

== Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders ==
{{Main|Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders}}
[[File:DSM-5 & DSM-IV-TR.jpg|thumb|The DSM IV and 5]]
The ''Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders'' (DSM) is a guideline for the diagnosis and understanding of mental disorders. The American Psychiatric Association (APA) sponsors the editing, writing, reviewing and publishing of this book. It is a reference book on mental health and brain-related conditions and disorders. It serves as reference for a range of professionals in medicine and mental health in the United States particularly. These professionals include psychologists, counsellors, physicians, social workers, psychiatric nurses and nurse practitioners, marriage and family therapists, and more. The current DSM is the fifth, most recent edition of this book. It was released in May 2013.<ref>{{Cite web |title=DSM-5: What It Is & What It Diagnoses |url=https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/articles/24291-diagnostic-and-statistical-manual-dsm-5 |access-date=2024-05-12 |website=Cleveland Clinic |language=en |archive-date=2023-12-30 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231230021825/https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/articles/24291-diagnostic-and-statistical-manual-dsm-5 |url-status=live }}</ref> Each edition makes significant changes to the classification of disorders.

== Research Domain Criteria ==
{{Main|Research Domain Criteria}}

The RDoC framework is a set of research principles for investigating mental disorders. It is meant to create a new approach to mental illness that leads to better diagnosis, prevention, intervention, and cures. It is not necessarily meant to serve as a diagnostic guide or replace the DSM, however, it is meant to examine various degrees of dysfunction. It was developed by the US National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH).<ref>{{Cite web |title=About RDoC - National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) |url=https://www.nimh.nih.gov/research/research-funded-by-nimh/rdoc/about-rdoc |access-date=2024-05-12 |website=www.nimh.nih.gov |language=en}}</ref> It aims to address heterogeneity by providing a more symptom based framework for understanding mental disorders. It relied on dimensions that span the range from normal to abnormal and allows investigators to work with a larger database. It uses six major functional domains to examine neurobehavioral functioning. Different aspects of each domain are represented by constructs which are studied along the full range of functioning. Together all of the domains form a matrix that could represent research ideas. It is a heuristic, and acknowledges that research topics will change and grow as science emerges.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Research Domain Criteria (RDoC) - National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) |url=https://www.nimh.nih.gov/research/research-funded-by-nimh/rdoc |access-date=2024-05-12 |website=www.nimh.nih.gov |language=en |archive-date=2026-03-11 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260311162156/https://www.nimh.nih.gov/research/research-funded-by-nimh/rdoc |url-status=live }}</ref>

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Rumination (psychology)
======================================================================

{{Short description|Focused attention on one's mental distress}}
{{Other uses|Rumination (disambiguation)}}
{{use dmy dates|cs1-dates=ly|date=November 2022}}
[[File:Dattatreya nadahalli.jpg|thumb|Rumination is related to [[worry]].]]

'''Rumination''' is the sustained focus on and repetition of negative thoughts and emotions.{{sfn|Salamon|2024}}{{sfn|Vigliotti|2024}}<ref name="Cambridge_Dictionary"/><ref name="Merriam-Webster"/> There are various psychological models of [[rumination]], which focus on different aspects: negative emotions and/or the circumstances surrounding that emotion; discrepancies between one's current and desired status; and the negative themes of uncontrollability and harm in metacognitions.

Rumination is a mechanism that develops and sustains [[psychopathology|psychopathological]] conditions such as anxiety, depression, and other mental states.{{sfn|Li et al. (2022)}} Multiple tools exist to measure ruminative thoughts. Treatments specifically addressing ruminative thought patterns are still in the early stages of development.{{sfn|Feldhaus et al. (2020)}} However, recent meta analyses of randomized-controlled trials suggest that psychological interventions including [[mindfulness]] and mindfulness-based interventions can significantly reduce rumination.<ref name="Wei2025"/><ref name="Mao2023"/><ref name="Baghmalek2026"/><ref name="VargasNieto2024"/><ref name="Perestelo-Perez"/>

==Definition==
Popularly defined, rumination is "an endless repetition of a negative thought or theme that spirals downward",{{sfn|Salamon|2024}} or an "endless loop of reрetitive thoughts аnd worries".{{sfn|Vigliotti|2024}} Dictionary definitions of rumination include:
* Cambridge Dictionary: "the act of thinking carefully and for a long period about something"<ref name="Cambridge_Dictionary">Cambridge Dictionary, [https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english/rumination Rumination]</ref>
* Merriam-Webster: "to go over in the mind repeatedly and often casually or slowly"<ref name="Merriam-Webster">Merriam-Webster, [https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/rumination Rumination]</ref>

Scholarly definitions include:
* Response Styles Theory: a form of coping with [[Self-discrepancy theory|self-discrepancy]] in which one focuses on [[Self-reference effect|self-referent]] thoughts and emotions instead of goal-directed action.{{sfn|Matthews|Wells|2004}} {{sfn|Nolen-Hoeksema|2008}} 
*Goal Progress Theory: "the tendency to think recurrently about important, higher order goals that have not yet been attained" or towards which sufficient progress has not been made.{{sfn|Smith|Alloy|2009}}{{sfn|Martin|Shrira|Startup|2004}}

==Occurrence==

===Variations===
Some common thoughts that are characteristic of ruminative responses are questioning the well-being of oneself and focusing on the possible causes and consequences of one's depressive symptoms.{{sfn|Nolen-Hoeksema|1991}} For example, some ruminative thoughts include "why am I such a loser", "I'm in such a bad mood" or "I just don't feel like doing anything".{{sfn|Nolen-Hoeksema|1991}}

Several variations of rumination can be distinguished in various types or forms:
* State rumination: dwelling on the consequences and feelings associated with the failure. State rumination is more common in people who are pessimistic, [[neuroticism|neurotic]], and who have negative [[attributional style]]s.<ref name="Sarason et al. (1996)">{{cite book | veditors = Sarason I, Sarason B, Pierce G | chapter = Mental rumination and learned helplessness: Cognitive shifts during helplessness training and their behavioral consequences. | title = Cognitive interference: Theories, methods, and findings | pages = 191–210 | vauthors = Mikulincer M | year = 1996 | location = Hillsdale, NJ | publisher = Lawrence Erlbaum }}</ref>
* Action rumination: task-oriented thought processes focused on goal-achievement and correction of mistakes.<ref name="Sarason et al. (1996)" /> 
* Task-irrelevant rumination: utilizing events or people unassociated with the blocked goal to distract a person from the failure.<ref name="Sarason et al. (1996)" /><ref>{{Cite journal |doi = 10.1521/jscp.2010.29.10.1057|title = Some Good News About Rumination: Task-Focused Thinking After Failure Facilitates Performance Improvement|journal = Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology|volume = 29|issue = 10|pages = 1057–1073|year = 2010| vauthors = Ciarocco NJ, Vohs KD, Baumeister RF |s2cid = 14689415}}</ref>
* Post-event processing: pervasive detailed reviewing of socially failed or embarrassing activities or situations that subjects perceive even more negatively/anxiety-provoking than they were, and they reinforce with pervasive recollections of similarly biased memories.{{sfn|Clark|Wells|1995}}<ref name="Fehm et al. (2003)">{{cite journal |vauthors=Fehm L, Schneider G, Hoyer J |date=2007 |title=Is post-event processing specific for social anxiety? |journal=Journal of Behavior Therapy and Experimental Psychiatry |volume=38 |issue=1 |pages=11–22 |doi=10.1016/j.jbtep.2006.02.004|pmid=16730328 }}</ref>
* Stress-reactive rumination: a pervasive detailed reviewing of painful experiences that specific stressful events induced and a [[cognitive bias]] enhances by memorising these events generally more stressful that they were while triggering depression.{{sfn|Robinson|Alloy|2003}}<ref name="Rood et al. (2012)">{{cite journal |vauthors=Rood L, Roelofs J, Bögels M |date=2012 |title=Stress-reactive rumination, negative cognitive style, and stressors in relationship to depressive symptoms in non-clinical youth |journal=Journal of Youth and Adolescence |volume=41 |issue=4 |pages=414–425 |doi=10.1007/s10964-011-9657-3|pmid=21451946 |pmc=3298737 |s2cid=254740492 }}</ref>

=== Sex differences ===
According to [[Susan Nolen-Hoeksema]], women tend to ruminate when they are depressed, whereas men tend to distract themselves. This difference in response style was proposed to explain the higher rates of depression in women compared to men.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Nolen-Hoeksema S | title = Sex differences in unipolar depression: evidence and theory | journal = Psychological Bulletin | volume = 101 | issue = 2 | pages = 259–282 | date = March 1987 | pmid = 3562707 | doi = 10.1037/0033-2909.101.2.259 | s2cid = 5026228 }}</ref> Research has supported the theory that women have a greater likelihood to ruminate than men, but the magnitude of this difference seems to be small.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Johnson |first1=Daniel P. |last2=Whisman |first2=Mark A. |date=2013 |title=Gender differences in rumination: A meta-analysis |journal=Personality and Individual Differences |volume=55 |issue=4 |pages=367–374 |doi=10.1016/j.paid.2013.03.019 |pmid=24089583 |pmc=3786159 |issn=0191-8869}}</ref> The prediction that men are more likely to distract themselves has not been consistently supported in research.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Strauss J, Muday T, McNall K, Wong M |year=1997 |title=Response Style Theory revisited: Gender differences and stereotypes in rumination and distraction |journal=Sex Roles |volume=36 |issue=11/12 |pages=771–792 |doi=10.1023/A:1025679223514 |s2cid=142916986}}</ref>

A [[meta-analysis]] was performed on both the sex differences in rumination of adults and the rumination subtypes "brooding" and "reflection." Studies show that women's chances of experiencing depressive symptoms or depression was twice that of men. The response styles theory (RST) suggests this may be due, to some extent, to higher rates of rumination in women. Brooding can be operationalized as continuous, passive, negative internalized thoughts. It is highly connected to worsening depression. Reflection is neutral, rather than negative, more active observation of self. In the meta-analysis, women showed [[Statistical significance|statistically significant]] increases in levels of both brooding and reflection, supporting RST. Interestingly, there was a much smaller sex difference in reflection than brooding. The meta-analyses found similar results across multiple study designs.<ref name="Gender differences in rumination: A">{{cite journal |vauthors=Johnson DP, Whisman MA |date=August 2013 |title=Gender differences in rumination: A meta-analysis |journal=Personality and Individual Differences |volume=55 |issue=4 |pages=367–374 |doi=10.1016/j.paid.2013.03.019 |pmc=3786159 |pmid=24089583}}</ref>

=== Healthy self-disclosure ===
Although rumination is generally unhealthy and associated with depression, thinking and talking about one's feelings can be beneficial under the right conditions. According to Pennebaker, healthy [[self-disclosure]] can reduce distress and rumination when it leads to greater insight and understanding about the source of one's problems.<ref>{{Cite book | doi=10.1016/S0065-2601(08)60309-3| chapter=Confession, Inhibition, and Disease| title=Advances in Experimental Social Psychology| volume=22| pages=211–244| date=1989 | vauthors = Pennebaker JW | isbn=978-0-12-015222-3}}</ref> Thus, when people share their feelings with others in the context of supportive relationships, they are likely to experience growth. In contrast, when people repetitively ruminate and dwell on the same problem without making progress, they are likely to experience depression. [[Co-rumination]] is a process defined as "excessively discussing personal problems within a dyadic relationship",<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Rose AJ | title = Co-rumination in the friendships of girls and boys | journal = Child Development | volume = 73 | issue = 6 | pages = 1830–1843 | date = 2002 | pmid = 12487497 | doi = 10.1111/1467-8624.00509 }}</ref> a construct that is relatively understudied in both its negative and positive trade-offs.

===Pathology===
Extensive research on the effects of rumination, or the tendency to [[Self-reflection|self-reflect]], shows that the negative form of rumination (associated with [[dysphoria]]) interferes with people's ability to focus on problem-solving and results in dwelling on negative thoughts about past failures.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Lyubomirsky S, Kasri F, Zehm K |year=2003 |title=Dysphoric rumination impairs concentration on academic tasks |journal=Cognitive Therapy and Research |volume=27 |issue=3| pages=309–330 |doi=10.1023/A:1023918517378| s2cid=14204781}}</ref> Evidence from studies suggests that the negative implications of rumination are due to cognitive biases, such as memory and attentional biases, which predispose ruminators to selectively devote attention to negative stimuli.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Joormann J, Dkane M, Gotlib IH |title=Adaptive and maladaptive components of rumination? Diagnostic specificity and relation to depressive biases |journal=Behavior Therapy |volume=37 |issue=3 |pages=269–280 |date=September 2006 |pmid=16942978 |doi=10.1016/j.beth.2006.01.002 |url=http://www.psy.miami.edu/faculty/jjoormann/publications/joormann_dkane_gotlib_2006.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140601005616/http://www.psy.miami.edu/faculty/jjoormann/publications/joormann_dkane_gotlib_2006.pdf |archive-date=2014-06-01 }}</ref>

The organic causes of rumination are not fully understood. Research has identified the activation of certain regions in the brain's [[default mode network]]s as [[neural substrate]]s of rumination, but the number of brain-imaging studies on rumination is limited.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Zhou |first1=Hui-Xia |last2=Chen |first2=Xiao |last3=Shen |first3=Yang-Qian |last4=Li |first4=Le |last5=Chen |first5=Ning-Xuan |last6=Zhu |first6=Zhi-Chen |last7=Castellanos |first7=Francisco Xavier |last8=Yan |first8=Chao-Gan |date=2020 |title=Rumination and the default mode network: Meta-analysis of brain imaging studies and implications for depression |journal=NeuroImage |volume=206 |article-number=116287 |doi=10.1016/j.neuroimage.2019.116287 |pmid=31655111 |s2cid=204837753 |issn=1053-8119|doi-access=free }}</ref>

The tendency to negatively ruminate is a significant risk factor for clinical depression.<ref name="Moulds2025">{{cite journal |last1=Moulds |first1=M. L. |last2=McEvoy |first2=P. M. |date=2025 |title=Repetitive negative thinking as a transdiagnostic cognitive process |journal=Nature Reviews Psychology |volume=4 |issue=2 |pages=127–141 |doi=10.1038/s44159-024-00399-6}}</ref>  Not only are habitual ruminators more likely to become depressed, but experimental studies have demonstrated that people who are induced to ruminate experience greater depressed mood.<ref name="Nolen-Hoeksema_1993"/> There is also evidence that rumination is linked to general anxiety, post traumatic stress, [[binge drinking]], eating disorders, and self-injurious behavior.{{sfn|Nolen-Hoeksema|Wisco|Lyubomirsky|2008}} Research suggests that rumination is somewhat associated with a higher frequency of [[Self-harm|non-suicidal self-injury]], and more heavily associated with a history of non-suicidal self injury.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Coleman |first1=Sophie E. |last2=Dunlop |first2=Brendan J. |last3=Hartley |first3=Samantha |last4=Taylor |first4=Peter J. |date=2021-11-22 |title=The relationship between rumination and NSSI: A systematic review and meta-analysis |journal=British Journal of Clinical Psychology |volume=61 |issue=2 |pages=405–443 |doi=10.1111/bjc.12350 |pmid=34806214 |s2cid=244519847 |issn=0144-6657 |url=https://research.manchester.ac.uk/en/publications/77f7db90-ef11-4a1e-ad94-0b421b961d41 }}</ref>

Rumination was originally believed to predict the duration of depressive symptoms. In other words, ruminating about problems was presumed to be a form of [[memory rehearsal]] which was believed to actually lengthen the experience of depression. The evidence now suggests that although rumination contributes to depression, it is not necessarily correlated with the duration of symptoms.{{sfn|Nolen-Hoeksema|Wisco|Lyubomirsky|2008}}

Research on the relationships between [[executive functions]] and rumination has yielded mixed results. Some studies have observed a negative [[correlation]] with two executive functioning abilities, [[Task switching (psychology)|set-shifting]] and inhibition, but the magnitudes of those relationships are unclear.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Yang |first1=Yingkai |last2=Cao |first2=Songfeng |last3=Shields |first3=Grant S. |last4=Teng |first4=Zhaojun |last5=Liu |first5=Yanling |date=2016-07-05 |title=The relationships between rumination and core executive functions: A meta-analysis |journal=Depression and Anxiety |volume=34 |issue=1 |pages=37–50 |doi=10.1002/da.22539 |pmid=27378739 |s2cid=27626857 |issn=1091-4269|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Vălenaș |first1=Sergiu P. |last2=Szentágotai-Tătar |first2=Aurora |date=2017-09-01 |title=The relationship between rumination and executive functions: A meta-analysis |journal=Journal of Evidence-Based Psychotherapies |volume=17 |issue=2 |pages=23–52 |doi=10.24193/jebp.2017.2.2 |issn=2360-0853}}</ref> Another study observed only one relationship between rumination and one executive function, specifically the ability to discard past information from [[working memory]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Zetsche |first1=Ulrike |last2=Bürkner |first2=Paul-Christian |last3=Schulze |first3=Lars |date=2018-06-07 |title=Shedding light on the association between repetitive negative thinking and deficits in cognitive control – a meta-analysis |doi=10.31234/osf.io/bz2ck |website=PsyArXiv|s2cid=242102055 |url=https://psyarxiv.com/bz2ck/ |url-access=subscription }}<br/>{{cite journal |first1=Ulrike |last1=Zetsche |first2=Paul-Christian |last2=Bürkner |first3=Lars |last3=Schulze |title=Shedding light on the association between repetitive negative thinking and deficits in cognitive control – A meta-analysis |journal=Clinical Psychology Review |volume=63 |date=2018 |pages=56–65 |issn=0272-7358 |doi=10.1016/j.cpr.2018.06.001|pmid=29913351 |s2cid=49313189 |url=https://psyarxiv.com/bz2ck/ |url-access=subscription }}</ref> Other studies, however, found no relationship between rumination and working memory.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" />

==Theories==
There are various models of rumination which focus on different aspects:
* negative emotions and/or the circumstances surrounding that emotion: Responsive Styles Theory, rumination on sadness model, five-factor model,{{sfn|Trapnell|Campbell|1999}} negative [[cognitive style]] model,{{sfn|Robinson|Alloy|2003}} social phobia model;{{sfn|Clark|Wells|1995}} 
* discrepancies between one's current and desired status: goal progress theory, conceptual evaluative model of rumination;
* the negative themes of uncontrollability and harm in metacognitions.{{sfn|Nolen-Hoeksema|Wisco|Lyubomirsky|2008}}

===Response styles theory===
Response styles theory (RST) initially defined rumination as passively and repetitively focusing on one's symptoms of depression and the possible causes and consequences of these symptoms.{{sfn|Papageorgiou|Wells|2004}} As evidence for this definition, rumination has been implicated in the development, maintenance, and aggravation of both depressive symptoms,<ref name="Nolen-Hoeksema_1993">{{cite journal |vauthors=Nolen-Hoeksema S, Morrow J |year=1993 |title=Effects of rumination and distraction on naturally occurring depressed mood |journal=Cognition and Emotion |volume=7 |issue=6 |pages=561–570 |doi=10.1080/02699939308409206}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Nolen-Hoeksema S, Parker LE, Larson J |title=Ruminative coping with depressed mood following loss |journal=Journal of Personality and Social Psychology |volume=67 |issue=1 |pages=92–104 |date=July 1994 |pmid=8046585 |doi=10.1037/0022-3514.67.1.92}}</ref> as well as episodes of [[major depression]].<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Nolen-Hoeksema S |title=The role of rumination in depressive disorders and mixed anxiety/depressive symptoms |journal=Journal of Abnormal Psychology |volume=109 |issue=3 |pages=504–511 |date=August 2000 |pmid=11016119 |doi=10.1037/0021-843x.109.3.504 |s2cid=43090073}}</ref> Recently, RST has expanded the definition of rumination beyond depression to include passive and repetitive focus on the causes, consequences, and symptoms of one's distress in general. This change was made because rumination has been implicated in a host of disorders, not just depression.{{sfn|Smith|Alloy|2009}}{{sfn|Nolen-Hoeksema|Wisco|Lyubomirsky|2008}}

RST also contends that positive distraction is the healthy alternative to rumination, where focus is directed to positive stimuli instead of to distress.{{sfn|Nolen-Hoeksema|1991}} However, the literature suggests that positive distraction may not be as potent a tool as once thought.{{sfn|Smith|Alloy|2009}}{{sfn|Nolen-Hoeksema|Wisco|Lyubomirsky|2008}}

Specifically, the S-REF model defines rumination as "repetitive thoughts generated by attempts to cope with [[Self-discrepancy theory|self-discrepancy]] that are directed primarily toward processing the content of [[Self-reference effect|self-referent]] information and not toward immediate goal-directed action."{{sfn|Matthews|Wells|2004}} Put more simply, when a person ruminates, they aim to answer questions such as:
* How do I feel about this event?
* How can I change my thoughts and feelings about the event?
* How can I prevent disturbing thoughts and feelings in the future?
However, in answering these questions, ruminators tend to focus on their emotions (i.e., "self-referent information") as opposed to [[problem solving]] (i.e., "goal-directed action").{{sfn|Matthews|Wells|2004}}

[[Meta-cognition]] is also an important part of the S-REF model and helps to explain the link between rumination and depression.{{sfn|Papageorgiou|Wells|2004}} Specifically, those who hold "positive meta-cognitive beliefs" about rumination (to make sense of negative thoughts and emotions or ensure the prevention of the same)<ref name="Papageorgiou_2001">{{cite journal | vauthors = Papageorgiou C, Wells A | year = 2001 | title = Positive beliefs about depressive rumination: Development and preliminary validation of a self-report scale | journal = Behavior Therapy | volume = 32 | issue = 1| pages = 13–26 | doi=10.1016/s0005-7894(01)80041-1}}</ref> are perhaps initially motivated to engage in rumination with high perseverance.<ref name="Papageorgiou_2003">{{cite journal | vauthors = Papageorgiou C, Wells A | year = 2003 | title = An empirical test of a clinical meta-cognitive model of rumination and depression | journal = Cognitive Therapy and Research | volume = 27 | issue = 3| pages = 261–273 | doi = 10.1023/A:1023962332399 | s2cid = 23020041 }}</ref> However, individuals who have engaged themselves in positive acts of rumination were more likely to use rumination as a coping mechanism upon encountering negative emotions. This causes the individual to modify their perception of rumination as unpleasant, unmanageable and "socially damaging" in general.<ref name="Papageorgiou_2003" /><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Papageorgiou C, Wells A | year = 2001 | title = Meta-cognitive beliefs about rumination in recurrent major depression | journal = Cognitive and Behavioral Practice | volume = 8 | issue = 2| pages = 160–164 | doi=10.1016/s1077-7229(01)80021-3}}</ref> Rumination additionally has a tendency to magnify with an [[Upregulation (psychology)|up-regulation]] <!--see talk page about this red link--> of emotions in the body, thus beginning the downward-moving spiral of depression.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Nejad AB, Fossati P, Lemogne C | title = Self-referential processing, rumination, and cortical midline structures in major depression | journal = Frontiers in Human Neuroscience | volume = 7 | page = 666 | date = October 2013 | pmid = 24124416 | pmc = 3794427 | doi = 10.3389/fnhum.2013.00666 | doi-access = free }}</ref> The individual's "negative meta-cognitive" beliefs then contribute to the development and maintenance of depression.<ref name="Papageorgiou_2003" />

===Goal progress theory===
[[Goal progress theory]] (GPT), sometimes referred to as Control Theory, seeks to explain rumination as a function of goal progress. Specifically, GPT views rumination as an example of the [[Zeigarnik effect|Zeigarnik Effect]], which suggests that individuals are more likely to remember information from unfinished tasks than from finished tasks.{{sfn|Watkins|2008}}{{sfn|Smith|Alloy|2009}} From this understanding, GPT defines rumination as "the tendency to think recurrently about important, higher order goals that have not yet been attained" or towards which sufficient progress has not been made.{{sfn|Smith|Alloy|2009}}{{sfn|Martin|Shrira|Startup|2004}}

GPT predicts that individuals for whom goal-related information is highly accessible should be more likely to ruminate. Various studies have provided support for this prediction.{{sfn|Watkins|2008}} However, the rumination experienced is focused more towards problem solving than rumination described by RST.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Roberts H, Watkins ER, Wills AJ | title = Cueing an unresolved personal goal causes persistent ruminative self-focus: an experimental evaluation of control theories of rumination | journal = Journal of Behavior Therapy and Experimental Psychiatry | volume = 44 | issue = 4 | pages = 449–455 | date = December 2013 | pmid = 23810947 | doi = 10.1016/j.jbtep.2013.05.004 | hdl = 10871/33114 | hdl-access = free }}</ref>

== Measurement ==
There are multiple tools for measuring rumination. These include the following:

The tendency to ruminate can be assessed with the Ruminative Responses Scale of the Response Styles Questionnaire.{{sfn|Nolen-Hoeksema|1991}}<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Bernstein EE, Heeren A, McNally RJ | title = Reexamining trait rumination as a system of repetitive negative thoughts: A network analysis | journal = Journal of Behavior Therapy and Experimental Psychiatry | volume = 63 | pages = 21–27 | date = June 2019 | pmid = 30590225 | doi = 10.1016/j.jbtep.2018.12.005 | s2cid = 58536838 | hdl = 2078.1/208986 | hdl-access = free }}</ref> On this measure, people are asked to indicate how often they engage in 22 ruminative thoughts or behaviors when they feel sad or blue.

The Rumination On Sadness Scale is a self-report tool consisting of 13 items that uses the [[Likert Scale]] to measure rumination of sadness.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Roelofs J, Muris P, Huibers M, Peeters F, Arntz A | title = On the measurement of rumination: a psychometric evaluation of the ruminative response scale and the rumination on sadness scale in undergraduates | journal = Journal of Behavior Therapy and Experimental Psychiatry | volume = 37 | issue = 4 | pages = 299–313 | date = December 2006 | pmid = 16678121 | doi = 10.1016/j.jbtep.2006.03.002 | url = https://cris.maastrichtuniversity.nl/en/publications/32979b47-e7be-41f9-9757-3a14bffc8e27 }}...</ref>

The 31-item Repetitive Thinking Questionnaire (RTQ) measures worry, rumination, and post-event processing with the purpose of controlling for effects associated with a psychological diagnosis or disorder. It includes two subscales, Repetitive Negative Thinking (RNT) and Absence of Repetitive Thinking (ART). RNT is associated with anxiety, depression, and other negative emotions as it influences metacognitive beliefs, cognitive avoidance strategies, and maladaptive thought control strategies.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Mahoney AE, McEvoy PM, Moulds ML |title=Psychometric properties of the Repetitive Thinking Questionnaire in a clinical sample |journal=Journal of Anxiety Disorders |volume=26 |issue=2 |pages=359–367 |date=March 2012 |pmid=22204788 |doi=10.1016/j.janxdis.2011.12.003}}</ref> The ART subscale reflects the absence of those negative emotions associated with the RNT subscale, essentially measuring their opposites.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=McEvoy |first1=Peter M. |last2=Mahoney |first2=Alison E.J. |last3=Moulds |first3=Michelle L. |date=2010 |title=Are worry, rumination, and post-event processing one and the same? |journal=Journal of Anxiety Disorders |volume=24 |issue=5 |pages=509–519 |doi=10.1016/j.janxdis.2010.03.008 |pmid=20409676 |issn=0887-6185}}</ref>

The Rumination-Reflection Scale involves 24 items. Half of the questions look for adaptive reflective thought while the other half note self-rumination focus. This scale incorporates the Likert Scale.<ref>{{Cite journal | vauthors = Janssen R |date=2021-02-01 |title=The Pleated Dress of Nywty |journal=PalArch's Journal of Archaeology of Egypt / Egyptology |volume=17 |issue=1 |pages=1–11 |doi=10.48080/jae.v17i1.3 |s2cid=234010733 |issn=1567-214X|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Recently, researchers have started to develop a validated measurement protocol to best assess rumination in a dynamic fashion using experience sampling methodology.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hoebeke |first1=Yorgo |last2=Blanchard |first2=M Annelise |last3=Contreras |first3=Alba |last4=Heeren |first4=Alexandre |date=2022 
|title= An Experience Sampling Measure of the Key Features of Rumination|journal=Clinical Neuropsychiatry|volume=19 |issue=5 |pages=288–297 |doi=10.36131/cnfioritieditore20220504 |pmid=36340270|pmc=9597648 }}</ref>

== Treatment ==

=== Rumination-focused cognitive behavioral therapy (RFCBT) ===
Some studies have begun developing a type of [[cognitive behavioral therapy]] that focuses on rumination.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Watkins |first1=Ed |last2=Scott |first2=Jan |last3=Wingrove |first3=Janet |last4=Rimes |first4=Katharine |last5=Bathurst |first5=Neil |last6=Steiner |first6=Herbert |last7=Kennell–Webb |first7=Sandra |last8=Moulds |first8=Michelle |last9=Malliaris |first9=Yanni |date=2007 |title=Rumination-focused cognitive behaviour therapy for residual depression: A case series |journal=Behaviour Research and Therapy |volume=45 |issue=9 |pages=2144–2154 |doi=10.1016/j.brat.2006.09.018 |pmid=17367751 |hdl=10871/11164 |issn=0005-7967|hdl-access=free }}</ref> Rumination-focused cognitive behavior therapy (RFCBT) aims to teach patients to recognize when they begin to ruminate and ultimately re-frame the way they view themselves.{{sfn|Feldhaus et al. (2020)}} The theories behind RFCBT as a treatment for rumination emphasize the fact that rumination is a destructive habit, and is mostly due to an individual's abstract cognitive processing.<ref name=":3" /> The approach that a therapist takes is to work with their client to change their thoughts into a healthy style of thinking. Instead of clients allowing negative repetitive thoughts to take over their daily life, therapists suggest that they process them into constructive thinking, which are helpful, process-focused, and concrete thoughts.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Watkins |first=Edwards |title=Rumination-Focused Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy for Depression |publisher=Guilford Publications |year=2016 |isbn=978-1-4625-3604-7}}</ref> In practice, this can look like the therapist prompting a client to replace their abstract ruminating "why" questions with more concrete "how" questions, that can be more easily examined and answered.<ref name=":4" /> Support for these interventions has come from a multitude of studies, suggesting that implementation of both individualized and group RFCBT has been correlated with lower rumination in adolescents and young adults, both with and without major depression or anxiety disorders.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Jacobs |first1=Rachel H. |last2=Watkins |first2=Edward R. |last3=Peters |first3=Amy T. |last4=Feldhaus |first4=Claudia G. |last5=Barba |first5=Alyssa |last6=Carbray |first6=Julie |last7=Langenecker |first7=Scott A. |date=2016-11-23 |title=Targeting Ruminative Thinking in Adolescents at Risk for Depressive Relapse: Rumination-Focused Cognitive Behavior Therapy in a Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial with Resting State fMRI |journal=PLOS ONE |language=en |volume=11 |issue=11 |article-number=e0163952 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0163952 |doi-access=free |issn=1932-6203 |pmc=5120778 |pmid=27880789|bibcode=2016PLoSO..1163952J }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Topper |first1=Maurice |last2=Emmelkamp |first2=Paul M. G. |last3=Watkins |first3=Ed |last4=Ehring |first4=Thomas |date=2017-03-01 |title=Prevention of anxiety disorders and depression by targeting excessive worry and rumination in adolescents and young adults: A randomized controlled trial |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0005796716302352 |journal=Behaviour Research and Therapy |volume=90 |pages=123–136 |doi=10.1016/j.brat.2016.12.015 |pmid=28049069 |issn=0005-7967|hdl=10871/25380 |hdl-access=free |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

=== Mindfulness-based intervention (MBI) ===
As mentioned in the lead section, rumination associates with other negative mental health conditions. Depression is one of [[Mental disorder|mental diseases]] that are cause by genetic, environmental, and mental factors that experience ruminative thoughts.{{sfn|Li et al. (2022)}}{{Failed verification|reason=The cited source does not mention genetic causation.|date=August 2026}} [[Mindfulness]]-based intervention can decrease the symptoms of rumination, as demonstrated by several meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials.<ref name="Wei2025">{{cite journal |last1=Wei |first1=S. |last2=Qin |first2=W. |last3=Yu |first3=Z. |last4=Cao |first4=Y. |last5=Li |first5=P. |date=2025 |title=The effectiveness of mindfulness-based cognitive therapy on rumination and related psychological indicators: a systematic review and meta-analysis |journal=BMC Psychology |volume=13 |issue=1 |pages=968 |doi=10.1186/s40359-025-03348-x |doi-access=free |pmid=40859383 |pmc=12382274 }}</ref><ref name="Mao2023">{{cite journal |last1=Mao |first1=L. |last2=Li |first2=P. |last3=Wu |first3=Y. |last4=Luo |first4=L. |last5=Hu |first5=M. |date=2023 |title=The effectiveness of mindfulness-based interventions for ruminative thinking: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials |journal=Journal of Affective Disorders |volume=321 |issue=Pt A |pages=83–95 |doi=10.1016/j.jad.2022.10.021 |pmid=36265738}}</ref><ref name="Baghmalek2026">{{cite journal |last1=Baghmalek |first1=A. K. |last2=Mahigir |first2=F. |date=2026 |title=Meta-analysis of the Effectiveness of Mindfulness-Based Interventions on Rumination: A Systematic Review of Iranian Trials |journal=International Journal of Education and Cognitive Sciences |volume=7 |issue=3 |pages=1–12 |doi=10.61838/kman.ijecs.7.3.1 |doi-broken-date=22 August 2026 }}</ref><ref name="VargasNieto2024">{{cite journal |last1=Vargas-Nieto |first1=J. |last2=Zambrano |first2=D. |last3=Montorio |first3=I. |last4=Sanabria |first4=L. M. |date=2024 |title=Efficacy of digital mindfulness-based interventions for repetitive negative thinking: A systematic review and bibliometric analysis |journal=Mindfulness |volume=15 |issue=3 |pages=523–538 |doi=10.1007/s12671-024-02313-1 |doi-broken-date=22 August 2026 }}</ref><ref name="Perestelo-Perez"/> The process of mindfulness based intervention is: (1) the interest in acceptance, (2) the defusion of thoughts and emotions, (3) the importance of being in the [[present|present moment]], (4) self as context. These mechanisms gives the ability to not suppress or avoid emotions but to encounter them without giving judgment.<ref name="Perestelo-Perez">{{Cite journal |last1=Perestelo-Perez |first1=Lilisbeth |last2=Barraca |first2=Jorge |last3=Peñate |first3=Wenceslao |last4=Rivero-Santana |first4=Amado |last5=Alvarez-Perez |first5=Yolanda |date=September 2017 |title=Mindfulness-based interventions for the treatment of depressive rumination: Systematic review and meta-analysis |journal=International Journal of Clinical and Health Psychology |volume=17 |issue=3 |pages=282–295 |doi=10.1016/j.ijchp.2017.07.004 |issn=1697-2600 |pmc=6220915 |pmid=30487903}}</ref>

Further, research has shown that psychological stress and other negative emotions activate physiological pathways involved in the stress response including the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis, with rumination on stressors repeatedly reactivating these responses.<ref name="Kaplan2018">{{cite journal |last1=Kaplan |first1=D. M. |last2=Palitsky |first2=R. |last3=Carey |first3=A. L. |last4=Crane |first4=T. E. |last5=Havens |first5=C. M. |last6=Medrano |first6=M. R. |display-authors=et al |date=2018 |title=Maladaptive repetitive thought as a transdiagnostic phenomenon and treatment target: an integrative review |journal=Journal of Clinical Psychology |volume=74 |issue=7 |pages=1126–1136 |doi=10.1002/jclp.22585 |pmid=29388207 |pmc=6003842}}</ref><ref name="VargasUricoechea2024">{{cite journal |last1=Vargas-Uricoechea |first1=H. |last2=Castellanos-Pinedo |first2=A. |last3=Urrego-Noguera |first3=K. |last4=Vargas-Sierra |first4=H. D. |last5=Pinzón-Fernández |first5=M. V. |last6=Barceló-Martínez |first6=E. |display-authors=et al |date=2024 |title=Mindfulness-based interventions and the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis: a systematic review |journal=Neurology International |volume=16 |issue=6 |pages=1552–1584 |doi=10.3390/neurolint16060113  |doi-access=free|pmid=39728560 |pmc=11670984}}</ref><ref name="Szabo2022">{{cite journal |last1=Szabo |first1=Y. Z. |last2=Burns |first2=C. M. |last3=Lantrip |first3=C. |date=2022 |title=Understanding associations between rumination and inflammation: A scoping review |journal=Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews |volume=135 |issue=3 |article-number=104523 |doi=10.1016/j.neubiorev.2022.104523 |pmid=35032549 |pmc=8851246 }}</ref> In contrast, the present-moment focus cultivated through mindfulness meditation appear to attenuate this process.<ref name= Karunamuni2021 >{{cite journal | vauthors = Karunamuni N, Imayama I, Goonetilleke D | title = Pathways to well-being: Untangling the causal relationships among biopsychosocial variables | journal = Social Science & Medicine | volume = 272 | article-number = 112846 | date = March 2021 | pmid = 32089388 | doi = 10.1016/j.socscimed.2020.112846 | s2cid = 211262159 | url = https://osf.io/dfu59/ }}</ref><ref name="Pascoe2017">{{cite journal | vauthors = Pascoe MC, Thompson DR, Jenkins ZM, Ski CF | title = Mindfulness mediates the physiological markers of stress: Systematic review and meta-analysis | journal = Journal of Psychiatric Research | volume = 95 | pages = 156–178 | date = December 2017 | pmid = 28863392 | doi = 10.1016/j.jpsychires.2017.08.004 }}</ref><ref name="Perestelo-Perez"/>

Specifically, the process of [[Mindfulness-based stress reduction]] (MBSR) has been generally correlated with lower rumination symptoms in both patients with various mental disorders and healthy patients.<ref name=":3" /> This process includes practices like meditation, body scans, and other nonjudgmental methods, mainly focusing on breath and passing thoughts. These practices can help individuals either let their ruminating thoughts arise and pass, or reduce dwelling on them, gently redirecting attention onto a present-moment meditation object such as the breath.<ref name=":3" /><ref name="KabatZinn2013">{{cite book |last=Kabat-Zinn |first=J. |date=2013 |title=Full Catastrophe Living: Using the Wisdom of Your Body and Mind to Face Stress, Pain, and Illness |publisher=Bantam Dell |location=New York |isbn=978-0-345-53972-4}}</ref>

== Relationship to other related constructs ==
Rumination has been confounded with other similar constructs that may overlap with it. Worry, negative automatic thoughts, and avoidance are a few of them.

=== Worry ===
Rumination appears closely related to worry. Some models consider rumination to be a type of worry (S-REF).{{sfn|Smith|Alloy|2009}} Worry has been identified as "a chain of thoughts and images, negatively affect-laden and relatively uncontrollable; it represents an attempt to engage in mental problem solving on an issue whose outcome is uncertain, but contains the possibility of one or more negative outcomes."{{sfn|Smith|Alloy|2009}}<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Borkovec TD, Robinson E, Pruzinsky T, DePree JA | title = Preliminary exploration of worry: some characteristics and processes | journal = Behaviour Research and Therapy | volume = 21 | issue = 1 | pages = 9–16 | date = 1983 | pmid = 6830571 | doi = 10.1016/0005-7967(83)90121-3 }}</ref>

Worry is often studied in the context of [[generalized anxiety disorder]] (GAD), whereas rumination is often studied in the context of [[major depressive disorder]]. Because of the high [[comorbidity]] of these two conditions, more recent research is exploring the overlap of worry and rumination.{{sfn|Smith|Alloy|2009}}

According to the [[Mental Health Foundation]], rumination has been identified to be one of the main problems that leads to anxiety and depression. A study conducted by psychologists from the [[University of Liverpool]] suggests that dwelling on negative events that have occurred in one's life is the biggest predictor of depression and anxiety.<ref>{{cite news | vauthors = Winterman D |title=Rumination: The Danger of Dwelling |work=BBC News |date=17 October 2013 |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/magazine-24444431 |access-date=2022-01-21 }}</ref>

Measures of rumination and worry have also demonstrated high correlations, above and beyond that of symptom measures of anxiety and depression (r=.66; Beck & Perkins, 2001).<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Beck |first1=R |last2=Perkins |first2=T. S. |date=2001 |title=Cognitive Content-Specificity for Anxiety and Depression: A Meta-Analysis |doi=10.1023/A:1012911104891 |journal=Cognitive Therapy and Research |volume=25 |issue=6 |pages=651–663 |s2cid=30854969 |via=SpringerLink}}</ref> Rumination and worry overlap in their relationships to anxiety and depression, although some studies do indicate specificity of rumination to depression and worry to anxiety. Rumination has been found to predict changes in both depression and anxiety symptoms and individuals with major depression have been reported to engage in levels of worry similar to individuals with GAD. As a whole, these studies suggest that rumination and worry are related not only to each other, but also each is related to symptoms of both depression and anxiety.

Other studies have demonstrated that the content of worry and rumination are distinct; worry thoughts are often focused on problem-solving and have a [[future orientation]], whereas ruminative thoughts concern themes of loss and are more focused on the past. Rumination, as compared to worry, has also been associated with less effort and less confidence in problem solving (Papageorgiou & Wells, 2004). It has also been suggested that rumination and worry serve different purposes, namely that rumination is associated with greater belief in the personal relevance of a situation and a larger need to understand it, whereas worry is associated with a desire to avoid worry thoughts (Watkins 2004b). Worry has also been hypothesized to contain more imagery than rumination; however, support for this has been mixed.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=McLaughlin KA, Borkovec TD, Sibrava NJ |title=The effects of worry and rumination on affect states and cognitive activity |journal=Behavior Therapy |volume=38 |issue=1 |pages=23–38 |date=March 2007 |pmid=17292692 |doi=10.1016/j.beth.2006.03.003}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |title=Process and meta cognitive dimensions of depressive and anxious thoughts and relationships with emotional intensity|journal=Clinical Psychology and Psychotherapy |year=1999 |volume=5 |issue=2 |page=152 |doi=10.1002/(sici)1099-0879(199905)6:2<156::aid-cpp196>3.0.co;2-a| vauthors=Papageorgiou C, Wells A}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Watkins E, Moulds M, Mackintosh B |title=Comparisons between rumination and worry in a non-clinical population |journal=Behaviour Research and Therapy |volume=43 |issue=12 |pages=1577–1585 |date=December 2005 |pmid=16239152 |doi=10.1016/j.brat.2004.11.008}}</ref>

Overall, these studies suggest that worry and rumination are related constructs that both lead to depression and anxiety. It is likely that rumination and worry, as with rumination and reflection, are related types of [[automatic negative thoughts|repetitive negative thinking]] that may be better captured as subtypes of some larger construct, such as avoidant coping strategies.

=== Automatic negative thoughts ===
Rumination has been compared to [[Automatic Negative Thoughts|automatic negative thoughts]], defined as repetitive thoughts that contain themes of personal loss or failure.

Nolen-Hoeksema (2004) contends that rumination (as defined in RST) is distinct from negative automatic thoughts in that while automatic negative thoughts are relatively shorthand appraisals of loss and depression in depression, rumination consists of longer chains of repetitive, recyclic, negative and self-focused thinking that may occur as a response to initial negative thoughts.<ref name=":4">{{Cite book |doi = 10.1002/9780470713853.ch6|chapter = The Response Styles Theory|title = Depressive Rumination: Nature, Theory and Treatment|pages = 105–123|year = 2004| vauthors = Nolen-Hoeksema S |isbn = 978-0-470-71385-3| veditors = Papageorgiou C, Wells A |location=West Sussex|publisher= John Wiley & Sons}}</ref> Nolen-Hoeksema also suggests that rumination may, in addition to analysis of symptoms, causes, and consequences, contain negative themes like those in automatic thoughts. Similarly, Papageorgiou and Wells (2004) have provided support to this conclusion when they found that rumination can predict depression even when negative cognitions are controlled, suggesting that these constructs do not wholly overlap and have different predictive value.{{sfn|Matthews|Wells|2004}}

Despite Nolen-Hoeksema's (2004) argument that rumination and negative automatic thoughts are distinct phenomena, the Response Style Questionnaire has been criticized for its conceptual overlap with negative automatic thoughts.

=== Avoidance ===
Avoidance can overlap with the habit of rumination, particularly because rumination is an avoidant action in itself.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=Rumination and related constructs: causes, consequences, and treatment of thinking too much {{!}} WorldCat.org |url=https://search.worldcat.org/title/1151903568 |access-date=2024-10-20 |website=search.worldcat.org |language=en}}</ref> Simply because the action of actively avoiding certain thoughts is difficult to achieve without ending up in rumination, the very practice of thought avoidance can increase rumination, even though the idea of avoiding thoughts and ruminating on them seem to be in complete opposition.<ref name=":3" />  There is evidence to support this idea, with studies supporting the fact that unsuccessful attempts to suppress particular thoughts are significantly related with strong rumination tendencies in some individuals.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ryckman |first1=Nathan A. |last2=Lambert |first2=Anthony J. |date=2015-01-01 |title=Unsuccessful suppression is associated with increased neuroticism, intrusive thoughts, and rumination |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0191886914005315 |journal=Personality and Individual Differences |volume=73 |pages=88–91 |doi=10.1016/j.paid.2014.09.029 |issn=0191-8869|url-access=subscription |hdl=2292/30064 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

=== Comorbid disorders ===
Research has determined that rumination is highly correlated with various psychiatric disorders.<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal |last1=Rickerby |first1=Nicole |last2=Krug |first2=Isabel |last3=Fuller-Tyszkiewicz |first3=Matthew |last4=Forte |first4=Elizabeth |last5=Davenport |first5=Rebekah |last6=Chayadi |first6=Ellentika |last7=Kiropoulos |first7=Litza |date=June 2024 |title=Rumination across depression, anxiety, and eating disorders in adults: A meta-analytic review. |url=https://doi.apa.org/doi/10.1037/cps0000110 |journal=Clinical Psychology: Science and Practice |language=en |volume=31 |issue=2 |pages=251–268 |doi=10.1037/cps0000110 |issn=1468-2850|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":6">{{Cite journal |last1=Watkins |first1=Edward R. |last2=Roberts |first2=Henrietta |date=2020-04-01 |title=Reflecting on rumination: Consequences, causes, mechanisms and treatment of rumination |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0005796720300243 |journal=Behaviour Research and Therapy |volume=127 |article-number=103573 |doi=10.1016/j.brat.2020.103573 |pmid=32087393 |issn=0005-7967|hdl=10871/40934 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Disorders related to high rumination behaviors include major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, [[social anxiety disorder]], and [[anorexia nervosa]].<ref name=":5" /> Individuals struggling with these disorders, when compared to individuals with no mental health issues, reported higher rates of rumination.<ref name=":5" /> In addition to these, individuals with [[obsessive–compulsive disorder]] (OCD) experience rumination as a [[Compulsive behavior|compulsion]], meaning individuals compulsively ruminate over thoughts and worries related to their obsessions.<ref name=":6" /> Rumination is considered one of the central cognitive symptoms of [[scrupulosity]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Miller |first1=Chris H. |last2=Hedges |first2=Dawson W. |title=Scrupulosity disorder: An overview and introductory analysis |journal=[[Journal of Anxiety Disorders]] |volume=22 |issue=6 |date=2008 |doi=10.1016/j.janxdis.2007.11.004 |pages=1042–1058 |pmid=18226490 |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0887618507002022 |url-access=subscription}}</ref>{{rp|1045}} People with [[borderline personality disorder]] may ruminate extensively about their interpersonal challenges, exacerbating negative emotions.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Peters |first1=Jessica |title=Characteristics of Repetitive Thought Associated with Borderline Personality Features: A Multimodal Investigation of Ruminative Content and Style |journal=Journal of Psychopathology and Behavioral Assessment |date=2017-02-23 |volume=39 |issue=3 |pages=456–466 |doi=10.1007/s10862-017-9594-x |pmid=28983149 |pmc=5624311 }}</ref>

'''Schizophrenia''' is a [[mental disorder]]<ref>{{cite web |title=ICD-11: 6A20 Schizophrenia |url=https://icd.who.int/browse11/l-m/en#/http%3a%2f%2fid.who.int%2ficd%2fentity%2f1683919430 |publisher=[[World Health Organization]] |access-date=23 August 2022}}</ref><ref name= Lancet2016/> characterized variously by [[hallucination]]s (typically, [[Auditory hallucination#Schizophrenia|hearing voices]]), [[delusion]]s, [[thought disorder|disorganized thinking]] or behavior,<ref name=DSM5/> and [[Reduced affect display|flat]] or [[inappropriate affect]].<ref name= Lancet2016/> Symptoms [[Prodrome|develop gradually]] and typically begin during young adulthood.<ref name=NIH2022/><ref name=DSM5/><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Tramazzo |first1=Sara |last2=Lian |first2=Wenxuan |last3=Ajnakina |first3=Olesya |last4=Carlson |first4=Gabrielle |last5=Bromet |first5=Evelyn |last6=Kotov |first6=Roman |last7=Jonas |first7=Katherine |title=Long-Term Course of Remission and Recovery in Psychotic Disorders |journal=American Journal of Psychiatry |volume=181 |issue=6 |date=2024-06-01 |issn=0002-953X |doi=10.1176/appi.ajp.20230189 |doi-access=free |pages=532–540 |pmid=38745457 |pmc=12884555 |url=https://osf.io/yh74r/ |access-date=2025-05-23}}</ref> There is no objective diagnostic test; diagnosis is based on observed behavior, a [[psychiatric history]] that includes the person's reported experiences, and reports of others familiar with the person.<ref name=DSM5/> For a [[Diagnosis of schizophrenia|formal diagnosis]], the described symptoms need to have been present for at least six months (according to the [[DSM-5]]) or one month (according to the [[ICD-11]]).<ref name=DSM5>{{cite book |title=Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders: DSM-5 |edition=5th |date=2013 |publisher=American Psychiatric Association |location=Arlington, VA |isbn=978-0-89042-555-8 |pages=99–105}}</ref><ref name=Ferri2019/> Many people with schizophrenia have other mental disorders, especially [[Mood disorder|mood]], [[Anxiety disorder|anxiety]], and [[Substance use disorder|substance use]] disorders, as well as [[obsessive–compulsive disorder]] (OCD).<ref name=DSM5/>

<!-- Epidemiology and causes -->
The [[lifetime prevalence]] of schizophrenia is about 0.3% to 0.7%.<ref name=Javitt2014>{{cite journal |vauthors=Javitt DC |title=Balancing therapeutic safety and efficacy to improve clinical and economic outcomes in schizophrenia: a clinical overview |journal=The American Journal of Managed Care |volume=20 |issue=8 Suppl |pages=S160-165 |date=June 2014 |pmid=25180705}}</ref> In 2017, there were an estimated 1.1&nbsp;million new cases and in 2022 a total of 24 million cases globally.<ref name=WHO2022/><ref name=GBD2018>{{cite journal |vauthors=James SL, Abate D |title=Global, regional, and national incidence, prevalence, and years lived with disability for 354 diseases and injuries for 195 countries and territories, 1990–2017: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2017 |journal=[[The Lancet]] |date=November 2018 |volume=392 |issue=10159 |pages=1789–1858 |doi=10.1016/S0140-6736(18)32279-7 |pmid=30496104 |pmc=6227754 |bibcode=2018Lanc..392.1789J}}</ref> Males are more often affected and on average have an earlier onset than females.<ref name=WHO2022>{{cite web |title=Schizophrenia Fact sheet |url=https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/schizophrenia |publisher=[[World Health Organization]] |date=10 January 2022 |access-date=23 August 2022 |archive-date=27 March 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190327174732/https://www.who.int/mental_health/management/schizophrenia/en/ |url-status=live}}</ref> The causes of schizophrenia may include [[Heredity|genetic]] and [[Environmental factor|environmental]] factors.<ref name=Lancet2016/> Genetic factors include a variety of common and rare [[Human genetic variation|genetic variants]].<ref name=vandeLeemput2016>{{cite book |vauthors=van de Leemput J, Hess JL, Glatt SJ, Tsuang MT |date=2016 |title=Genetics of Schizophrenia: Historical Insights and Prevailing Evidence |series=Advances in Genetics |volume=96 |pages=99–141 |doi=10.1016/bs.adgen.2016.08.001 |pmid=27968732 |isbn=978-0-12-809672-7}}</ref> Possible environmental factors include [[Risk factors of schizophrenia#Urbanicity|being raised in a city]], childhood adversity, [[Cannabis (drug)|cannabis]] use during adolescence, infections, the [[Advanced_maternal_age|age of a person's mother]] or [[Paternal age effect|father]], and poor [[Prenatal nutrition|nutrition during pregnancy]].<ref name=Lancet2016/><ref name=Parakh2013/>

<!-- Course and prognosis -->
About half of those diagnosed with schizophrenia will experience improvement over the long term with no further relapses, and a small proportion of these will recover completely.<ref name=DSM5/><!-- Quote: "The course appears to be favorable in about 20% of those with schizophrenia, and a small number of individuals are reported to recover completely." --><ref name=Vita2018>{{cite journal |vauthors=Vita A, Barlati S |s2cid=35299996 |title=Recovery from schizophrenia: is it possible? |journal=Current Opinion in Psychiatry |date=May 2018 |volume=31 |issue=3 |pages=246–255 |doi=10.1097/YCO.0000000000000407 |pmid=29474266}}</ref> The other half will have a lifelong impairment.<ref name=Law2015>{{cite book |vauthors=Lawrence RE, First MB, Lieberman JA |chapter=Chapter 48: Schizophrenia and Other Psychoses |veditors=Tasman A, Kay J, Lieberman JA, First MB, Riba MB |title=Psychiatry |edition=fourth |date=2015 |pages=798, 816, 819 |doi=10.1002/9781118753378.ch48 |publisher=John Wiley & Sons, Ltd. |isbn=978-1-118-84547-9}}</ref> In severe cases, people may be admitted to hospitals.<ref name=Vita2018/> Social problems such as [[long-term unemployment]], poverty, [[homelessness]], exploitation, and victimization are commonly correlated with schizophrenia.<ref name=Killaspy2014/><ref name=Charleson2018>{{cite journal |vauthors=Charlson FJ, Ferrari AJ, Santomauro DF, Diminic S, Stockings E, Scott JG, McGrath JJ, Whiteford HA |title=Global Epidemiology and Burden of Schizophrenia: Findings From the Global Burden of Disease Study 2016 |journal=Schizophrenia Bulletin |volume=44 |issue=6 |pages=1195–1203 |date=October 2018 |pmid=29762765 |pmc=6192504 |doi=10.1093/schbul/sby058}}</ref> Compared to the general population, people with
